This research paper explores a control problem that involves the dissemination equation in a highly random environment, specifically the equation $dU(t)=\sqrt{t}U(t)^2dt+U(t)dW(t)$ with the goal of minimizing $U^2(t)$. Unlike similar control problems, this one lacks a natural boundary condition. To address this issue, a new type of boundary condition is introduced that is based on the random variable $U(1)$. The main focus of this paper is to examine a specific discretization method and its impact on a related optimization problem that involves a random process. The optimization problem in question occurs over a time period from $0$ to $1$ and includes a complex equation of the form \begin{equation*} \begin{cases} dU(t)= f(U(t),t)dt + g(U(t),t)dW(t)\\ U(0)=0\\ U(1)=0. \end{cases} \end{equation*} The discretization method being studied involves dividing the time interval $[0,1]$ into $N$ equal parts and defining the process $U_j(N)$ for $j=0,...,N$ using the recursive formula \begin{equation*} U_j(N) = U_{j-1}(N) + f(U_{j-1}(N),\tau_j) \tau_j + g(U_{j-1}(N),\tau_j) (W(\tau_j) - W(\tau_{j-1})) \end{equation*} The authors also investigate the relationship between the values $U_j(N)$ and the optimization problem mentioned above, and determine that the values $U_j(N)$ converge to the solution of the control problem as the time interval $[0,1]$ becomes increasingly divided. The authors further demonstrate that the specific discretization method being studied is equivalent to a new class of optimization problems that involve the random process $W(\tau_j)$ for $j=0,...,N$. The paper also includes an appendix that provides an alternative method of solving the control problem mentioned above using a different type of boundary condition based on the random variable $U(1)$. The authors further demonstrate that the specific discretization method being studied is equivalent to a new class of optimization problems that involve the random process $W(\tau_j)$ for $j=0,...,N$. The paper also includes an appendix that provides an alternative method of solving the control problem mentioned

This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - solvability - which arises from a more general property called nilpotency. Specifically, we have found that there is an interval $n$, dependent on the algebra's base field, such that any $n$-step derivation fulfills the role of a natural scalar multiplication, thereby making the algebra $n$-step solvable. If the base field is symmetric, then the algebra becomes completely solvable. Additionally, we have established that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a field that is not algebraically closed is solvable, whereas over an algebraically closed field, there are solvable yet nonsimple Zinbiel algebras. A particular example is provided to illustrate this conclusion. Lastly, we have established that the quotient operation by which Zinbiel algebras are simplified yields algebras that are equivalent in spirit to Malcev algebras and more specifically, to Basmalcev algebras, though with the condition that the original algebra has a specific property called the weak division property. A particular field $(\mathbb{F}_3, \text{weak division})$ is identified where simple algebras cannot be obtained through this quotient operation, thereby giving an affirmative answer to a previously unconfirmed conjecture made by Van den Berken. A solvability test is also described in this paper. Moreover, a specific and known result from the literature on the ideals of a solvable Zinbiel algebra is presented, along with an alternative and independently derived proof. Our research examines impact parameter variations' effect on rare meson decays that develop into charged particles at the LHC. Rare meson decays into charged particles have a well-defined time frame in which the direction of the decay is influenced by the velocity of the decaying particle rather than overall collision flow. Utilizing LHC data from lead-lead collisions at a 5.02 TeV collision energy, we found the angle between the decay direction and the overall collision flow to be approximately 20 degrees, depending on impact parameter and transverse momentum. Additionally, we found transverse momentum ratios between particle and antiparticle decays to be nearly indistinguishable, with differences of less than 5%. The magnitude of the decay angle is found to increase with higher transverse momentum, and is consistent with the effect of initial angular momentum in collisions. The potential of this phenomenon for revealing hidden properties of rare mesons is also discussed. The measured effect of impact parameter and initial angular momentum on decay direction may have implications for quark matter composition in the central region of lead-lead collisions. In complex scenes, objects often overlap, making it difficult to establish correspondences between points on different objects. To tackle this challenge, we introduce Neural Description Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that incorporates a neural network providing an explicit definition of an object's local structure, in addition to a contrastive learning-based field that identifies objects within a scene. We enforce the field's equivariance to an object's local structure under rigid transformations, ensuring that corresponding points on the same object retain the same relationship despite rotational or translational differences. Through extensive experiments on multiple datasets involving both 2D and 3D scenes with partially overlapping objects, NDFs consistently outperforms baseline methods in correspondence prediction, segmentation, and 3D reconstruction tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/PRM-TU-Darmstadt/Neural-Description-Fields.

Using functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order, we have verified that the Yang-Lee singularity remains critical for all O(N) symmetric $\phi^4$ theories with the constraint removed, specifically within the parameter range where the symmetry is broken into the $z$-axis. Our analysis confirms that the critical behavior at the Yang-Lee edge aligns with the Landau-like universality class for all values of $N$, particularly in the context of second-order phase transitions where the mean field region of parameter space exhibits two independent order parameters. We have also investigated the scenario where the symmetry is broken into the $z$-axis without the constraint removed, finding that the critical behavior at the Yang-Lee edge converges to the mean-field universality class for $N \geq 4$. In the process, we have established the conditions under which the universality class changes from the mean-field type to the Landau-like type. Moreover, our calculations have allowed us to determine the exact power laws describing fluctuations in the location and depth of the Yang-Lee singularity along trajectories in parameter space. These predictions can be tested through measurements of correlation lengths and critical amplitudes in lattice simulations of $\phi^4$ theories within the described regimes. These results also imply that the Yang-Lee edge cannot be mapped onto the Ising universality class, contrary to previous misinterpretation. The critical dimensions associated with the Yang-Lee edge are $d_c = 1 + \frac{N}{2}$ for structure factor calculations, and $d_c = 2 + \frac{N}{2}$ for correlation length calculations. The corresponding $\beta$-functions for these dimensions are $\beta_d = \frac{d_c}{48} \left( N + \frac{N^2}{2} \right)$. The predicted power laws can be tested through high-precision lattice simulations involving both Monte Carlo methods, particularly the multi-overrelaxation algorithm, and cumulant expansions. The predicted results will help validate the functional renormalization group approach used in this research. While using imaging cameras in astronomy can be beneficial for detecting aerosol effects on atmospheric visibility, they also pose challenges in quantifying aerosols due to limited access to camera characteristics. Researchers explored the application of photometric measurements in degrading image quality, assuming these degradations are similar to those caused by the atmosphere. By analyzing the effects on point spread functions (PSFs), researchers developed an alternative approach to determine the amount of turbulence and aerosol present. Contrary to traditional methods that focus on comparing images to reference standards, this method compares the actual PSFs generated during observations. As a result, this approach provides more precise information about the atmosphere during observations. Furthermore, researchers found that the extent of degradation required to match observed images contains valuable information about image formation processes and can be used to assess the performance of telescopes and instruments. By combining this information with models of atmospheric turbulence and aerosol, researchers can determine the quantity of aerosol present, calculating it as approximately 0.143 grams per liter for a particular observational case study. Additionally, researchers explored the relationship between this approach and traditional methods, concluding that both methods are interrelated and provide the same information about the atmosphere during observations. Overall, this research highlights the utility of photometric measurements in analyzing aerosol effects on the atmosphere and demonstrates that aerosol quantities can be determined from image degradation, relying solely on the characteristics of image formation processes. In robotics and computer vision applications, defining a robot's pose relative to its surroundings is crucial. This task involves determining six degrees of freedom (DoF): three for translation and three for rotation. Poses are often determined using images from a single camera, but this approach is prone to ambiguity and may result in multiple possible poses for a single image. This issue persists even with the latest deep learning-based methods, despite achieving high accuracy for individual images. To address this challenge, researchers typically rely on additional information, such as 3D point clouds or multiple images. In our previous work, a framework called DeepHMap was introduced, which utilizes a unique projection pathway to predict a 3D scene representation from images. This framework overcomes the ambiguity issue associated with single-image pose determination and enables the calculation of all six DoF. In this paper, we enhance the projection pathway of DeepHMap by introducing a clustering-based masking technique that reduces the impact of occluded features on the 3D scene representation. This technique results in a more precise and fully defined 3D scene representation, which in turn enables a single-image pose determination with four degrees of freedom. Furthermore, we introduce a correspondence learning module between the projected 3D scene and a set of predefined 3D models to validate the effectiveness of our framework for real-world applications. This module facilitates the calculation of all six DoF pose determinations without additional information. In our experiments, we demonstrate the efficacy of this framework on a public dataset and an indoor real-world dataset captured using a flying robot equipped with a multi-camera setup. In both cases, the accuracy of pose determination improves compared to our previous work and other state-of-the-art methods. In addition, we showcase the practical application of this framework on a flying robot by enabling it to navigate around an unknown environment for the first time. In our current implementation, we assume the availability of 3D models in advance, which is a common practice in various computer vision applications. In the future, we aim to develop a generalization of this framework that enables the automatic creation of 3D models from images, which would further enhance the practical usability of this method. In our analysis, we expanded the concept of eigenvector prominence to multi-layer networks. These networks consist of multiple interconnected graphs, each representing a separate domain. We then developed methods for calculating prominent nodes within each individual graph, as well as across the entire network, taking into account the relationships between the graph's significance and the connection between its components. Our approach allows us to determine the relative prominence of nodes across multiple layers and can be adjusted to accommodate various weighting schemes. By utilizing a weighted version of the method, we demonstrated how it can be applied to identify node dependencies and patterns of influence across the network. Furthermore, we found that our approach can be compared to existing prominence measures used in single-layer networks. Our research also explored a weighted scenario that accounts for changes in network dynamics over time. To apply this model to real-world data, we utilized a time-varying network of co-authorships between researchers. Our results showed that our method is effective in detecting the central nodes that contribute significantly to the network's stability and identity over time. Our research provides a versatile tool for network analysts that can be tailored to suit a variety of applications, including the study of multilayer networks consisting of categorical nodes. Our methodology is available online.

This study investigates how spheres interact with a liquid surface at moderate speeds, specifically in regimes where partial sealing occurs. High-speed cameras captured images of spheres moving through a liquid surface, with their trajectories and seal formation observed in various scenarios. A detailed analysis of these images provided insights into the spheres' movement, including their acceleration, deceleration, and reversal of direction. Furthermore, the images revealed patterns of water droplets that formed on the spheres' surfaces, and how they influenced sealing behavior. A key finding is that spheres moving through a liquid surface can experience multiple instances of sealing and unseling, even at high speeds. This study also identifies three distinct water droplet patterns that form on the spheres' surfaces, and how they affect sealing behavior. A key factor determining the spheres' movement and seal behavior is the tension in the liquid surface, which must be accounted for in future studies of sphere-liquid interactions. This report outlines our proposed approaches for creating and utilizing human-generated image descriptions to evaluate automatic description tools. We begin by describing a method for compiling a single diverse description for each image from a pool of descriptions provided by human references. A subsequent assessment strategy leveraging this diverse description is then detailed. It compares the overlap between a single automatically-generated description and the pool of human-provided descriptions, with the goal of accounting for the diversity of these descriptions. A preliminary evaluation of our proposed approaches using a dedicated dataset and evaluation tool is also presented. It compares our assessment method using both the original Fleiss delta metric and a new diversity-aware variant, to the existing approach of matching human-generated descriptions. The results indicate our new metric yields more accurate rankings of description tools, as reflected in their performance scores. It is our hope that making our description diversity-aware assessment approach publicly available will facilitate further improvements to existing evaluation tools and provide a foundation for future research. It is particularly relevant for datasets containing numerous human-generated descriptions. The code and additional details about our method are available at: https://github.com/ghritli/human-reference-assessment.

Cross-domain recommendation techniques are crucial for addressing the issue of sparse data that arises when recommending products to users who have minimal interaction history. Current methods often fall into three categories: selection, combination, and transformation strategies. However, these approaches have several limitations, such as overlooking user-specific aspect preferences, being overly reliant on target domains, and using unnecessary feature transformations. To address these shortcomings, this paper proposes a novel method called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation via Thorough Aspect Preference Learning (MSDCoAL). First, MSDCoAL uses separate models to derive separate preference vectors for each domain, then these models are combined into an overall aspect preference vector. Notably, MSDCoAL incorporates an adaptive sampling technique to focus on user interactions that are relevant to specific domains, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of target domain recommendations. The proposed method is evaluated in a real-world setting across three different target domains, and the results show that MSDCoAL outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of recommendation accuracy. Moreover, the paper demonstrates the scalability of MSDCoAL by conducting additional experiments using larger-scale datasets. The underlying methodology and algorithm of MSDCoAL are also compared to current methods through a comprehensive analysis of its key components such as user-specific aspect preferences, adaptive sampling, and feature transformation, which highlights the advantages of MSDCoAL. The open-source code of MSDCoAL is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhoukaihao1995/MSDCoAL. The proposed method can be applied to a wide range of real-world cross-domain recommendation scenarios, including e-commerce websites, online streaming platforms, and social media networks. Conic programming is an extension of linear and quadratic programming that allows for the representation of a wide variety of nonlinear phenomena, and it has been successfully applied in numerous optimization tasks, particularly those involving high-dimensional data, by employing organic conic formulations, which can be solved using modern conic solvers with guaranteed global convergence. However, there is no established method for automatically generating these organic conic formulations from nonlinear problems, and even simple examples, such as the log-function, cannot be formulated using traditional techniques. In this work, we introduce an original method for creating organic conic formulations based on an analysis of the conic representation of the log-function, and we provide general guidelines for forming these formulations for any conic that can be expressed in a composite or inherited form. As a result, any nonlinear function defined over non-negative variables can be formulated using these composite forms, and even those that cannot be formulated in such a way can be approximated by combining a small number of these forms. We have made this method available in the open-source Julia package Hypatia, which includes an interactive notebook for demonstrating the application of this method to the log-function and other examples, and we show that it is possible to generate formulations for a wide range of commonly encountered nonlinear functions, including the geometric mean, the harmonic mean, the entropy function, and the soft-plus function. Furthermore, we have included a discussion on the issues related to the enlargement of these formulations and their application to quadratic problems, and we have provided an analytical conic formulation for the log-function over the positive semi-definite variables. The advent of deep learning has significantly improved MRI image acquisition by allowing for the reduction or elimination of certain preparation steps, such as partial Fourier transformation, aliasing, and image acceleration techniques. In the context of brain MRI, these advancements have led to faster acquisition times. However, these faster methods often result in noisier images, which can negatively impact segmentation and analysis tools that rely on high-quality data. In order to utilize the benefits of faster MRI acquisition methods while maintaining the integrity of these tools, it is essential to develop a quality assurance protocol for MRI images. This protocol aims to assess and ensure that acquired images meet the requirements for accurate and reliable analysis through various applications. In this research, we leverage deep learning techniques to restore noisy MRI images acquired using faster methods, with the goal of replicating images that were obtained using traditional, higher-quality techniques. Specifically, we employed a U-Net based model to correct images acquired using specific faster MRI methods, with the goal of achieving comparable quality to images acquired using traditional techniques. This research was conducted in collaboration with a major hospital, involving approximately 2000 images acquired using different MRI protocols, in addition to multiple segmentation and analysis tasks. Our results demonstrate that even noisier images acquired using faster MRI methods can be restored to a level that is equivalent to images acquired using traditional techniques, with only a 10% drop in performance in various applications. In summary, we developed a simple and effective deep learning-based MRI image restoration protocol that enables the use of faster MRI acquisition methods without compromising the integrity of analysis tools. This protocol has the potential to accelerate MRI image acquisition without generating noisier images. In the context of brain MRI, this research offers numerous applications, including but not limited to, the use of faster acquisition techniques, partial Fourier transformation, aliasing, and image acceleration techniques, in addition to generalizations to other MRI acquisition methods, organs of interest, and other applications. In addition, we made our code and data available to the public through the following link: https://github.com/ghassan-k/brain-mri-image-restoration.

To understand how private electric vehicles influence the stability of electric power grids and improve distribution network resilience, this study utilizes a multi-agent optimization approach. It defines optimization problems at both an individual level (EV owner's scheduling problem) and a collective level (generator scheduling and dispatchable load formation problems). These problems are solved using three distinct methods: genetic algorithm, mixed-integer convex programming, and semi-definite programming. The research utilizes a simulated environment to validate the proposed framework and examines grid stability using two indicators: active power variation and imaginary power percentage. Furthermore, it investigates the impact of private EVs on grid stability during different resilience levels and finds that they can significantly enhance grid resilience with appropriate incentives. The study also discovers that private EVs' influence on the grid varies greatly and that a variety of factors including their location, charging/discharging behavior, and distance from transmission lines play critical roles. To better understand and quantify these factors' effects, the research develops two novel indicators: spatial distribution and temporal variation indices. It finds that distributing incentives randomly may lead to poor outcomes and that a targeted approach is more effective in promoting grid resilience. The study concludes that private EVs have a significant reservoir of energy that can be harnessed to manage grid instability and suggests several avenues for future research. The proposed framework and findings can be applied to other similar distributed resources that are currently underutilized, such as large industrial water storage tanks. The research assumes that EV owners' scheduling and grid stability optimization objectives can be achieved instantly, which may require further investigation given the complexity of these problems. The study also notes that real-world implementation may require the integration of additional factors including weather conditions, grid component status, and various societal and environmental constraints. The proposed framework provides a solid foundation for this integration. The research utilizes a simulated environment due to the unavailability of real-world data, which may affect the results' generalizability. The lack of accessible real-world data limits the analysis to a single test case, which may not represent all possible distribution network configurations. The research assumes that EV owners are fully incentivized and compliant with grid stability directives, which may not always be the case. The study suggests several avenues for future research into the dynamics of EV owner behavior and possible policies to manage it. The research assumes that the distribution network consists of a single branch, which may not accurately represent real-world distribution networks with multiple branches. The study suggests investigating how private EVs influence grid resilience in such networks. The research assumes that the availability of generator power and demand for electricity remains constant

At the core of DAMRM lies a Markov Decision Process framework, incorporating a decentralized learning approach through the application of multi-agent reinforcement learning. Our research involves an empirical investigation of DAMRM through simulated co-working scenarios among multiple agents, yielding promising outcomes in terms of optimized performance when compared to alternative methods, including centralized management and competitive coexistence. The model has also demonstrated versatility in scaling to accommodate an increased number of interacting agents. The foundation theorem for a Coxeter system initially gained prominence due to its utility in proving the exchange lemma, a fundamental result in the theory. It has since found broader applications, demonstrating its value in the study of (left) ideal lattices of Coxeter groups. This paper expands on this concept by establishing a new, more general version of the foundation theorem, applicable to infinite Coxeter groups of type B. Additionally, it provides a more specific, previously unknown result regarding the foundation theorem's application to n-dimensional Bn spaces, where n is two or greater. Moreover, it offers a direct proof of the exchange lemma's validity within Bn spaces, bypassing the foundation theorem. Finally, it shows that the foundation theorem's validity can be extended to infinite ideal lattices generated from Coxeter groups of type B. The paper also includes a relevant historical context, citing the foundational work of Dan Crawmer and Nicolas Berliaud. The concept of foundation has further implications, potentially in the study of group actions, as it enables the demonstration of the solvability of finite groups that act on a set of Bn spaces. The paper concludes by presenting two such examples of these actions. The paper's final section addresses the question of whether the foundation theorem can be applied to infinite Coxeter groups of type A. The paper offers one possible approach to answering this question, involving the use of Kurosh's method, although it cautions that this method may not yield a useful result. The paper also explores a related question concerning the foundation theorem's application to the finite universal Coxeter groups of type A, noting that it leads to the derivation of the exchange lemma's equivalent form, which is known as the length formula, as well as Derksen's and Brink's results regarding the ideal lattices generated from these groups. The paper's final result concerns the ideal lattices generated from the finite universal Coxeter groups of type B, demonstrating that its lattice is isomorphic to the set of all integers k such that 0 < k ≤ n. The paper notes that this result was previously known by Brink, although it presents a distinct proof of this fact. Reconstructing the distribution of Type Ia Supernovae (SNe Ia) through weak lensing convergence fields can provide valuable information to understand the structure of the universe. Conforming to its conservative approach, this study utilizes Pantheon SN Ia data and a simple model of cosmological projections to calculate the minimum level of cosmological information that can be obtained from weak lensing effects on SN Ia discoveries. A key factor in this calculation is the lensing influence from the surrounding matter, which is adequately represented by an all-sky model of galaxy halos based on the Milky Way. Determining the required depth and width of SN Ia surveys, this research demonstrates that collecting deep weak lensing effects on SN Ia discoveries is either infeasible with current satellite capabilities or requires a significant expansion of their field of view. Nevertheless, this study shows that even now, with existing SN Ia data and galaxy maps at hand, it's possible to recover valuable insights about the distribution of matter in the universe through the lensing effects on observed SN Ia events. Specifically, combining Pantheon SN Ia data with the CONDOR-S4 galaxy catalog yields a markov chain monte carlo sample of $10^4$ samples of the cosmological and lensing parameters, which recovers the true values with the following precision: scale matter density $\Omega_m = 0.2790^{+0.0081}_{+0.0081}$; the amplitude of matter fluctuations $\sigma_8 = 0.8120^{+0.0124}_{+0.0124}$; the lensing signal from galaxy halos around SN Ia discovery sites recovers the true value with a precision of a few percent, which is sufficient to justify more precise models of galaxy halos based on the Milky Way. This research also highlights the significance of incorporating the effects of the SN Ia discovery selection function on weak lensing effects, which can result in misinterpretation of cosmological data similar to how it misinterpreted the lensing effects on the Sloan Digital Sky Survey III SN Ia data. Finally, this study suggests that future SN Ia surveys, although may not collect deep weak lensing effects on SN Ia discoveries, can still derive highly precise estimates of the distribution of matter in the universe through the lensing effects on observed SN Ia events with a precision that is comparable to future satellite missions of the cosmic microwave background. This research was conducted in the framework of the Pantheon SN Ia data analysis

The development of efficient and compact light-matter interaction systems, both for quantum information applications and biophotonic sensing, relies heavily on effective methods to create sharp light resonance profiles. While achieving high resonance frequency, small light resonance widths, and strong light-matter interaction widths is crucial, it also presents a significant technological challenge. This issue can be resolved by utilizing a novel photonic semiconductor material called Silicon-on-Diamond (SoD), which leverages the interplay between diamond's abundant etch trenches to create precise light resonance patterns. A specific SoD structure, named T hubs, has been proposed, and its potential has been investigated through numerical modeling. The results show that T hubs are capable of delivering extremely narrow light resonance widths, exceeding 40 times thinner than the equivalent silicon structure, while maintaining high resonance frequencies above 300 THz. Furthermore, this novel SoD material and its T hubs structure have demonstrated robustness in the presence of disorder, ensuring that light resonance patterns remain unaffected by small diamond etch trenches. However, achieving a rationalizable equilibrium through iterative learning is complicated by competitions involving multiple players.  In such scenarios, it is necessary to determine how each player updates their strategy based on the gains they achieve in previous rounds.  We have discovered three key principles that must be followed in order to guarantee the convergence to a rationalizable equilibrium to be possible: (1) players must maintain a memory of previous rounds, (2) their learning process must be directed towards maximizing their gains in relation to the performance of other players, and (3) the set of available strategies must remain constant.  By applying these principles to various competition scenarios, we have found that the convergence to a rationalizable equilibrium is possible in some cases but not in others.  In particular, the convergence to a unique rationalizable equilibrium is possible when there are two players, but it is not possible when there are more than two players. These results can be interpreted as extensions of existing research on learning in multiagent competitions. In our analysis of chatbots and their limitations, we noticed that most systems
limit user choices to two options, making future conversations predictable.
To address this constraint, we present a new dialogue framework called
MultiTalk, which allows highly branching conversations and retains the benefit
of efficient two-option responses. In MultiTalk, the system can provide two
main types of answers: either two distinct possibilities, or a combined
option that presents two subchoices. We developed a simple training approach
for chatbot models using a combination of contrastive learning and a custom
loss function. Our evaluations revealed that MultiTalk models excel at both
branching and diversity tasks when compared to conventional dialogue systems. 
To demonstrate the versatility of our approach, we also explored variations
of the framework with limited success, including utilizing a different loss
function, integrating external knowledge, and employing different activation
functions. Our findings with a 128-tree test set indicated that the system
can frequently determine the correct path within as few three turns, or
approximately 25% of the total possible branches. To further assess the
system's performance under uncertain user inputs, we introduced random errors
into user responses, which showed that the system is highly resilient in such
scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/MultiTalk.

A new method of managing radio frequency (RF) energy and information within a wireless system that services multiple users has been proposed, known as Wireless Information and Power Transfer (WIPPT). This technology assigns different services to different services, some of which receive information and power through the same channel, and others that receive only information. To fully leverage the potential of WIPPT, it's crucial to understand how to effectively distribute limited resources, such as transmission power and bandwidth. This distribution has a significant impact on the services' performance, including their data transfer rates and the amount of energy harvested, and it's complicated by the varied and often conflicting requirements of different services. This research paper delves into the practical implementation of WIPPT, focusing on a system that uses separate channels for information and power transfer, and offers two viable alternatives: one that maximizes the harvesting efficiency of a single device, and another that optimizes the performance of multiple devices harvesting energy and receiving information simultaneously. A real-world example based on a 4G Long-Term Evolution (LTE) system is also provided to illustrate the potential of WIPPT and the complexity of its distribution problem. This has been approximated as an integer programming problem that can be solved efficiently, and several optimization approaches have been tested and compared, including a novel simple alternative. This research is an important step towards developing efficient and practical methods for managing the distribution of resources in WIPPT systems, and it offers a promising foundation for exploring further enhancements, such as adapting transmission power and bandwidth, and implementing energy and performance thresholds for services harvesting energy and receiving information. This has the potential to lead to a more sophisticated integer programming problem, possibly with conflicting objectives, and it would likely involve considering various performance indicators, capturing the dynamics of wireless systems, and investigating several optimization approaches, including but not limited to, metaheuristics, genetic algorithms, and simulated annealing. This technology has numerous applications, including enhancing the efficiency and performance of various wireless systems that harvest energy and transfer information, such as radio frequency identification (RFID) systems, cognitive radio systems, and multiple-service WIPPT systems. The detection of gravitational waves at high frequencies is constrained by the velocity limit of optical sensors and the laser noise. To overcome these limitations, we examine an alternative configuration based on a sloshing-Sagnit interferometer, where the movement of the free fluid determines the optical path difference. This design could potentially expand the bandwidth of optical sensors to frequencies previously thought off-limits. Utilizing numerical models, we have tested and validated a novel sensing scheme with a suspended fluid chamber, demonstrating that it can effectively convert gravitational wave information into an optical signal. By analyzing noise sources, we identify light-induced fluid motion as a dominant effect, but also discover that it can be minimized through a variety of means. Based on our simulations, we believe that a chamber with a diameter of 10 cm, filled with water, could optimize a detector like LIGO Plus for frequencies between 50 to 100 Hz, or with a smaller diameter of 5 cm, with water or mercury, for frequencies between 100 to 200 Hz. Although the conversion efficiency of this design is lower than traditional sensors, its unique characteristics make it an intriguing option for combining multiple signals, such as the motion of a massive mirror in an advanced detector, or as a means of detecting specific types of gravitational waves, like those with high frequency components. The concept of a sloshing-Sagnit interferometer also has applications in other fields, such as the monitoring of free surface flows, or in the study of turbulence. The potential integration of this design with other sensing configurations, along with its versatility in adapting to different fluids and sizes, make it a valuable discovery with a broad range of uses. In large-scale MIMO networks, researchers have identified overlapping cell patterns as a major performance limitation. To address this challenge, a stochastic access protocol was proposed, enabling random switching between overlapping and non-overlapping cell configurations. To ensure efficient macro-cell coverage, the access protocol conditions visible areas between cells not to overlap. Until now, research has focused on the statistical properties of overlapping areas without exploring the implications of non-overlapping areas. This study delves into the average and variance of non-overlapping area proportions between cells and reveals a positive correlation between these proportions and the signal power received from the serving cell. Furthermore, we found that the variance of the non-overlapping area proportions is directly proportional to the variance of the signal power received from the serving cell. Moreover, this study investigated the optimal cell configuration and found that the ideal non-overlapping area proportion varies significantly between different configurations, arising from the uneven distribution of users' locations and their corresponding signal power thresholds. To determine the optimal non-overlapping area proportion, we derived an explicit and general expression based on the underlying stochastic model, ensuring that the proposed stochastic access protocol conditions the non-overlapping areas not to intersect, and ensuring efficient macro-cell coverage. Therefore, this study contributes a precise and universal expression for the non-overlapping area proportion, enabling further optimization of the stochastic access protocol for improved performance. Lastly, this study investigated two particular scenarios, including a crucial case where the signal power threshold is infinite, and demonstrated that in this instance, the optimal non-overlapping area proportion converges to one, indicating that in this case, the proposed stochastic access protocol conditions the cells to be fully overlapping, which is an intuitively expected outcome. The derived expressions can be applied to further research on the stochastic access protocol, including the analysis of edge-cell configurations and the optimization of small-cell coverage. The findings of this study can be extended to evaluate the performance of other MIMO network configurations, including rectangular cell configurations and networks with multiple layers of cells. The research methods employed in this study are general and can be applied to a broad range of stochastic models and performance metrics, including other metrics such as the area proportion below a certain threshold or the distribution of users' locations within the cell configurations. The study of these metrics will provide further insights into the performance of MIMO networks and will contribute to a deeper understanding of the underlying stochastic models, enabling the optimization and evaluation of various network configurations, including cellular networks, device-to-device communication networks, and other applications that involve complex stochastic interactions between multiple entities. As a result, a range of motionless output modes become de facto identical, and a single gate operation can successfully convert one of these modes into a desired form. The development of an efficient frequency-resilient Molmer-Sorensen gate is a key aspect of this research, and it outperforms the optimal gate control protocol previously suggested for its frequency-insensitive counterpart. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our proposed technique demonstrates robustness in situations involving significant head poses and demonstrates the generative capability of the model by conducting a head-pose generation experiment. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/lingyu-gh/SADRNet. The resulting 3D face reconstructions and dense alignment results are shown in Figures 1-4 in the supplementary materials. The derived facial parameter maps enable real-time head-pose manipulation via the NeRFDemo tool, as displayed in Figure 5 in the supplementary materials. We analyze the effects of perturbations on an inflationary model based on a specific type of algebraic attractor potential, examining how it relates to the formation of primordial black holes. By incorporating the criteria for PBH formation, we determine the associated scalar perturbation scale. Our calculation considers the impact of scalar perturbations on the mass of PBHs, demonstrating that it can be minimized by adjusting the inflationary model's parameters. Furthermore, we investigate the connection between PBH formation and the characteristics of the cosmic microwave background, analyzing the observable consequences in CMB maps, particularly in the distribution of quadrupole moments. Our findings indicate that PBH formation primarily results from fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background at specific multipole moments, namely $\ell \approx 2$. Our analysis also suggests that the fraction of the universe composed of PBHs is too small to account for the observed dark matter density. Our predicted density spectra align with existing predictions derived from gravitational wave events, such as GW150914. Firstly, it can be seen as a sequence of characters where the order is significant, or secondly, it can be viewed as a set of characters paired with their respective positions within the tree. We have undertaken an analysis of this data structure within the framework of formal language theory. Specifically, we have investigated the properties of labeled ordered trees presented in an alphabet of three characters, denoted as A, B, and C, where the order of the characters is crucial. This paper introduces iOCR, a cutting-edge Informed Optical Character Recognition system specifically designed to accurately count votes in elections. iOCR utilizes a two-step process, initially employing a deep learning-based OCR technique to generate probable character spellings from scanned ballot images, and then matching these predictions against a trusted reference database to produce certain counts. We tested iOCR on a dataset comprising 10 different election ballot types and found it outperformed traditional OCR methods in both character recognition and counting accuracy. Furthermore, iOCR demonstrated robustness in handling various scanning resolutions and ballot font styles. Our experiments also highlighted the benefits of incorporating a reference database in informed OCR, suggesting this approach can be applied to various real-world applications beyond election ballot counting. The code for iOCR has been made publicly available on GitHub at the specified URL. We believe this work has implications for any organization that relies on accurate text extraction from documents containing formatting errors. The results from our evaluation of iOCR on election ballot counting have also been presented to election officials and they expressed interest in implementing this method in their voting processes. The current version of iOCR is sufficient for handling the election ballot counting task but there are opportunities to enhance the performance of iOCR further. The most obvious area for improvement is in increasing the efficiency of the reference database matching process against the massive number of possible spellings of scanned characters, which can be challenging even with the use of a powerful computing infrastructure. Another potential enhancement is in training the OCR model using election ballot fonts to further boost the character recognition accuracy. The code for iOCR has been designed to be adaptable to these and other modifications that may be necessary to handle other real-world applications involving informed OCR. The code for iOCR has been developed using Python 3 and relies on the following libraries: PyTIF, Pillow, numpy, scikit-learn, joblib, and gunicorn. The reference database used in iOCR is an exact match database that comprises the correct spellings of the text contained in the election ballots. This database was provided to us by the election officials and it is essential for the informed OCR process as it allows the system to differentiate between similar character spellings that may correspond to different text elements. The reference database is used in the informed OCR process to generate certain counts of the text elements on the ballot images. In recent years, over-parameterized models have gained significant attention, and their ability to handle noisy and outdated data has been found to be advantageous. This paper explores an over-parameterized linear regression scenario, where the optimization process is performed on a dataset that contains irrelevant information. The analysis shows that the model can still effectively exploit the informative data, despite the presence of misfitting. A key challenge in decentralized energy management systems arises from the lack of a trusted central authority to manage storage effectively, specifically in multi-period scenarios. This study addresses this issue by developing an automated planning function for individual energy consumers with private storage capacity. This planning function aims to minimize costs and ensure reliable energy supply during peak periods. A novel two-stage optimization approach underpins the solution, involving a straightforward subproblem that serves as a reference for the consumer's actions in the subsequent time period, and a more complex superstructure that accounts for various retention and discharge opportunities across the grid. A Dual-Projection Algorithm has been successfully applied to solve the intricate core problem of this self-contained framework. Furthermore, simulated testing in a real-world market setting utilizing the European Energy Exchange market data has demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach. The resulting cost and operational scheduling of the storage unit are credible references for other decentralized agents willing to transact in the market, providing a foundation for future work on trustless bargaining theories that could lead to more advanced storage management strategies. Researchers who utilize silicon's electron-spin interactions for quantum computing are concerned about the impact of exchange-related coupling between distant donor atoms, potentially causing computational errors. To address this issue, a new research framework is introduced that combines an all-encompassing simulation method and a semi-analytical theory to accurately assess configuration interactions in multi-photon experiments involving donors. The simulation tool, known as Multi-Valley Effective Weight Theory, employs a vast library of simulated data that includes all possible interactions and scattering of photons and electrons, and is effective in predicting the outcomes of such experiments, even with a large number of donors. To validate this framework, it was applied to a scenario that deviates from its intended purpose, and the results showed that it accurately replicates the findings of a previous study that used a different simulation approach. Furthermore, the tool was used to examine the influence of exchange-related coupling on a promising quantum computing protocol, and it was discovered that even a relatively distant donor atom, located 1.5 nanometers away from the central donor, can cause significant computational errors due to exchange-related coupling. To address this issue, the research paper proposes an alternative quantum computing protocol that is less susceptible to the effects of exchange-related coupling, and it was found that this new protocol is more efficient and less prone to computational errors caused by exchange-related coupling. The research paper also discussed the possibility of utilizing donors that are farther apart, which could be achieved by utilizing a different silicon material known as silicon-on-insulator. The research was conducted using a simulation tool that was developed for this purpose, and it was discovered that this tool can predict the outcomes of experiments with donors that are located up to 4 nanometers away from the central donor atom, which is sufficient for addressing the concerned issue. The research paper concluded by highlighting the importance of exchange-related coupling for future quantum computing applications, which could be achieved by developing methods to control this interaction, and it also discussed the possibility of utilizing donors that are located in close proximity to each other, which could be achieved by utilizing a different silicon material known as silicon-on-insulator. The research paper finished by emphasizing that the developed simulation tool provides unlimited predictive capabilities for any configuration of donors, which could be an overstatement, but it is certain that the tool provides a wide range of predictive capabilities for any configuration of donors. In recent years, advances in optimization methods and collaborative learning have relied on the widespread assumption that gradients can be freely exchanged between participants. However, securing gradient information raises significant security concerns. We propose a novel technique where participants exchange information about their internal neural network states, specifically using Hamiltonian Neural Networks, from which optimized gradient acquisition is possible without directly exchanging gradients. We also present an optimized version of this method that reduces communication between participants. Our proposed NNGD algorithm utilizes Hamiltonian Neural Networks as an intermediary to securely and efficiently obtain gradients for collaborative learning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by applying it to benchmark datasets in low-communication settings. Our findings show that our method achieves comparable results to conventional collaborative learning methods while significantly reducing communication expenses. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghru/hamiltonian-grad-acq.

AI models can sometimes rely on untrustworthy data, leading to poor performance and decreased reliability. To address this issue, we present a novel online framework called TADpole that addresses both the quality of the data and the level of trust placed in the model. TADpole assigns a trust rating to each data sample based on several factors, including but not limited to anomalous or missing features. It then uses a two-layer architecture to separate reliable and unreliable data, where the inner layer generates an initial degree of trust for each data point, and the outer layer updates both the model and the level of trust based on the quality of the data. As TADpole maintains both a database of reliable examples and a model, we view it as a multi-agent system consisting of a teacher agent that trains the model, a cleaner agent that ensures data cleanliness, and a validator agent that determines the level of trust. TADpole can be applied to a variety of tasks including but not limited to classification and detection. We present experimental results using real-world datasets to demonstrate the effectiveness of TADpole. The code for TADpole is available at https://github.com/ghulamai/TADpole. The proposed method outperforms existing reliable machine learning techniques and baseline models in most cases. The code for TADpole has been tested using real-world datasets including MNIST, CIFAR10, and a dataset of self-driving cars. The proposed method can be applied to various applications including but not limited to classification and detection of anomalies. We present a comparison of TADpole with existing reliable machine learning techniques and baseline models in the experimental results section. The results show that TADpole generally performs better than existing reliable machine learning techniques and baseline models in most cases. We consider a specific type of embedded surface in the form of a twisted tube in $T^2 \times I$, denoted as $\mathcal{S}_\theta$ with a volume hypothesis ratio of $\rho$ and twist angle of $\theta$. This surface meets three requirements: it has no boundary, its volume is within the volume hypothesis range, and its end surfaces are smoothly attached to the boundary of $T^2 \times I$. For a fixed volume hypothesis ratio $\rho$ greater than 1, we establish that the 2-dimensional incompressible surface invariant $\mathcal{J}_\rho(\mathcal{S}_\theta)$ increases with the twist angle $\theta$. Additionally, we demonstrate that there is no surface that minimizes the invariant under these constraints. Furthermore, we show that any surface with a twist angle less than $\theta$ or a ratio less than $\rho$ has a higher invariant than $\mathcal{J}_\rho(\mathcal{S}_\theta)$. In the special case where the surface has a ratio equal to 1, we demonstrate a similar relationship among the surfaces with the same volume. These findings extend and modify previous results by Michelsen and Britton, as well as Kombu-Ryu and Shoda. Lastly, we provide a lower bound for the invariant that includes a term related to the volume of the surface and demonstrate that this lower bound converges as the surface's volume increases, ultimately revealing that the invariant is directly proportional to the volume of the surface for surfaces with a volume hypothesis ratio greater than 1. This study focuses on key aspects of cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance the quality of parsed data, we introduce a dual-objective reinforcement learning model to precision and fluency, which significantly improves the performance of baseline models in both tasks. To create a suitable training environment, a simulated scenario is designed with adjustable difficulty levels, and we find it essential to establish a challenging framework that requires the model to accurately analyze complex schema links and value fills. To further advance baseline performance, we introduce an additional task called fill-filled prediction, which enhances output fluency and precision by training the model to distinguish between original and filled values. The evaluation reveals that our model outperforms baseline standards in cross-domain settings. To demonstrate applicability to different domains, we adapt our model to fill-filled prediction, which enables it to operate on domains where the value filling task has been completed. Consequently, our model achieves superior results compared to standard approaches in both schema linking and value filling tasks, as validated by human assessors. The findings from this research can be applied to various value filling scenarios, including but not limited to cross-domain settings. This paper delves into the world of structured data, specifically focusing on confidentiality for graph-based data structures that underlie numerous modern applications. We outline the fundamentals of graph data, its varying representations, and the types of queries that can be executed on it. We then examine differential confidentiality within graph data, exploring how to ensure the confidentiality of individual data elements while also maintaining the integrity of query results. We discuss the challenges of enforcing differential confidentiality on graph data, including efficient execution of queries and valid results in the presence of confidentiality constraints. We also review and analyze existing research on differential confidentiality for graph data, categorizing it by data representation and considering issues like the assumption of node behavior and whether or not nodes follow predefined query protocols. We conclude by outlining potential research directions, including exploring node-free graph data representations, developing decentralized systems that prioritize privacy and efficiency, and examining the relationship between differential confidentiality and data consistency. We hope this paper serves as a valuable reference for scholars and practitioners working with graph-based data and concerned about maintaining the confidentiality of individual data elements. The Euclid legacy will be enriched by the analytical data resulting from the telescopes and spacecraft. We outline the potential scientific benefits of utilizing former mission components, including the flight model of the visible and near-infrared spectroscopic instrument, a simulated version of the instrument on the Ground Test Model, the Euclid spacecraft itself, and the Occultation Sensor for Atmospheric Studies. We discuss three categories of scientific enquiries: astronomical, related to the Euclid mission itself, and atmospheric, focused on retrieving information from occultations of Earth's atmosphere. A prior assessment of Euclid's VISIR proved feasible with little modification, enabling rapid repurposing. A few examples of Euclid's capabilities are demonstrated, including the analysis of stellar spectra, investigation of the spacecraft and instrument, and the retrieval of atmospheric parameters during Earth occultations. Although primarily an heritage science opportunity, these studies also enhance the Euclid legacy through validated instrument performance and accurate measurements of the atmosphere. Despite some technical challenges, many scientific enquiries are available to Euclid heritage science with a relatively short development period. The phenomenon of form coherence in nuclear reactions is theoretically supported by the quark-meson model, particularly involving the $\omega$-meson, and is expected to be more conspicuous for monopole tensor interactions. To investigate this phenomenon, a study employs the quark-meson model to simulate the $\omega$-meson's mean-field interactions within 64Ni nuclei. Calculations focus on the coexistence of different forms (i.e., density distributions) resulting from the $\omega$-meson's coupling to either isoscalar-scalar or isovector-vector operators. To mimic conditions relevant to intermediate-energy reactions, the model includes both collective and non-collective 0+ states. By comparing the collective 0+ states formed through monopole tensor interactions with those involving the $\omega$-meson, this study aims to explore the ideal conditions under which form coherence emerges, and to investigate the relationship between this phenomenon and the $N\Delta$-multiplicity. As such, it also examines the influence of form coherence on the 0+ states' properties, such as their energy, charge density distributions, and $\gamma$-vibration energies. Furthermore, the study delves into the underlying physics by analyzing the distribution of the $\omega$-meson's density within the 64Ni nucleus, both in its ground and excited states, as well as investigating the role of the $N\Delta$-mechanism on form coherence and the associated $\gamma$-vibrational mode. Lastly, it discusses the implications of this research for interpreting experimental data obtained through (e,e'$\omega$) reactions, and its broader context within the study of form coherence in other nuclei. The model's applicability to this research is validated by comparing the calculated properties of 64Ni with empirical data, involving the measurement of electric monopole strengths, charge density distributions, and the energy of the $\gamma$-vibrational mode. The model's predictions for the energy of the 2+2$\gamma$ and 0+1 states, as well as the $\gamma$-vibrational mode's energy in 56Ni, are also examined. The study concludes by highlighting the importance of accounting for the $\omega$-meson's interactions with the NΔ degree of freedom, and suggesting that (e,e'$\omega$) reactions offer a promising means of investigating form coherence and the associated $\gamma$-vibrational mode within medium-mass nuclei. Machine learning models often benefit from tuning hyperparameters, a process that can be computationally intensive, particularly for models with significant training time, such as BERT. To adjust these models, researchers commonly employ grid search with k-fold cross-validation to balance precision and computational expense. However, this method's variance can hinder the effectiveness of its outcomes. To mitigate this issue, we suggest using the results of k-fold cross-validation as the basis for a grid search, narrowing the hyperparameter space before conducting a more thorough analysis on a different subset of the data. This streamlined approach yields both a more precise estimate and substantially reduced variance compared to conventional methods. Our experiments with real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed technique achieves superior performance at a significantly lower computational expense. Our findings also highlight the proposed method's advantages when coupled with other tuning methods. To facilitate further integration with existing tuning tools, we have publicly released our code alongside this paper. It is essential to note that our proposed technique is not specific to BERT, and our results show it can be effectively applied to a broad range of NLP models. Moreover, our findings suggest that the proposed method is particularly well-suited for datasets with limited training data. To further reduce the proposed method's variance, we recommend incorporating a simple ensemble of different random initializations of the K-Fold CV process. Our results demonstrate that this strategy, known as ENSEKCV, yields outstanding performance in nearly all cases, consistently outperforming a range of baseline models. ENSEKCV is remarkably effective at scaling the proposed method to large datasets, without compromising the significant reduction in variance it achieves. Our research highlights the critical role of random initialization in K-Fold CV, and the modest additional computational expense of ENSEKCV, makes it an extremely appealing option for a broad range of tuning tasks. Our results are accompanied by a comprehensive analysis of the proposed method's parameters, and a range of tuning techniques that can be effectively combined with ENSEKCV. Our research opens up a range of potential future research directions, including an in-depth statistical analysis of the variance and bias of K-Fold CV, as well as an exploration of the connections between ENSEKCV and other sampling techniques, such as stratified sampling. In recent years, significant progress in AI has led to advancements in teacher-student frameworks, which have numerous real-world applications such as knowledge acquisition, image classification, and natural language processing. These frameworks, characterized by an autonomous teacher generating training data for a student model, have proven efficient in producing high-quality training sets and adapting existing models to new tasks with minimal effort. The concept, however, has its roots in traditional machine learning techniques like semi-supervised learning and transfer learning. This review article surveys various forms of teacher-student frameworks, discusses their theoretical foundations, and examines their practical uses in popular tasks and datasets. Moreover, we outline existing challenges and potential solutions in the field, and conclude by highlighting future research directions and potential combinations of techniques that could lead to breakthroughs. With its versatile name, the teacher-student framework is referred to as instructor-pupil learning in this review.

In large-scale graphical models, calculating the most probable explanation (MPE) or performing structured optimization within a bounded space can be extremely time-consuming due to the massive amount of time spent on scanning through vast function domains. This issue can be overcome by a new approximation approach called Brief Function (BF) descriptions. This method represents each function as a compact, simplified model that retains only the most critical features for valid decision-making within the constrained context. Using BF descriptions, the search for the optimal output is then focused on a significantly more manageable subset of the original function space, resulting in a significant performance improvement. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this innovation through a range of experiments involving synthetic data and real-world applications, and show that BF descriptions can be integrated into existing algorithms with minimal modification, leading to a range of benefits including a substantial reduction in computation time, without sacrificing too much accuracy. Contrary to a traditional perspective that views this threshold as constant, our experiments on a range of particle sizes and densities within a confined space demonstrate that the scaling of shear rate is directly proportional to the scaling of particle size and density. This proportionality disrupts a previous assumption of a universally fixed stress ratio across different conditions and provides a framework for understanding the global and local breakdown of the shear-induced crust. Our findings also highlight the importance of considering both the height and the density of the particles in determining the shear-induced structure and our proposed scaling has been validated through comparisons with both the Hopper and the Plug flow regimes. Furthermore, our analysis reveals a constant acceleration characteristic of the shear-induced crust breakdown, a phenomenon that persists even across varying particle sizes and densities. This constant acceleration is a crucial feature that underlies the physics of the shear-induced crust and our results demonstrate that it is a fundamental aspect of the physics involved, rather than a result of specific or idealized conditions. Our proposed scaling has also been applied to similar problems of flow-induced sedimentation and crust breakdown that occur in a variety of natural and engineered settings, including rivers, ocean and sea beds, and layered materials. These settings share a common feature of having a complex geometry with varying depths of sedimentation and different densities of sediment layers. Our analysis has further found that the shear-induced structure of the sediment layers breaks down at a critical height that is directly proportional to the height of the layer, a finding that is supported by a range of experimental and natural examples. Our results provide a framework for understanding the complex geometry of shear-induced structure and the associated breakdown, a challenge that has been a major obstacle in predicting and modeling a variety of flows within confined and layered spaces. Customized web search results page rankings, a core feature of modern search engines, may lead to the exclusion of pertinent information from users' perception. This study quantifies the extent to which this phenomenon hinders a user's access to relevant information. Our investigators conducted an experiment in which 30 searchers on Google, native English speakers with graduate degrees, located scholarly articles related to a particular query. The outcomes revealed that approximately 20% of the searchers failed to discover a certain article, which ranked 10th or better on the results page, due to the web search engine's customization. This study also found that users' overlook of certain information is significantly more likely if it appears on the second page of results, with a predicted 12% to 23% probability. The research underlying this paper was designed to provide evidence that can be useful for developing suitable methods of web search customization, as well as for better comprehending the implications of customized results for users' access to knowledge. It is our hope that these findings will be beneficial to a wider range of stakeholders interested in web search customization and its consequences. A new, powerful accelerator is envisioned to surpass the capabilities of existing facilities by providing high-energy muons and heavy ions at high intensities. This complex, called MIRA for "Muon-Ion Accelerator," aims to bridge the gap in scientific research that current facilities cannot reach due to limitations in available particle intensities and energy levels. Researchers are exploring the potential of MIRA to drive breakthroughs in three key areas: 1) establishing the absolute value of the weak interaction,  2) revealing the unknown properties of matter, and  3) advancing medical and industrial applications through the development of new cancer treatments and materials characterization. To achieve this, MIRA will consist of three main components: a high-power electron accelerator, a target and a front-end that produces and accelerates ions and muons, and a series of accelerators and storage rings for optimizing particle energy, intensity, and storage capacity. By optimizing design and operational strategies, as well as exploring new technologies, MIRA is expected to offer significant scientific, medical, and industrial benefits while also driving innovation in accelerator technology and inspiring educational opportunities. Although the technical challenges are substantial, the potential rewards make this ambitious project worthwhile. Given its scope and magnitude, collaboration with international teams and researchers is crucial to the success of MIRA. Although initial estimates place the total construction cost at approximately $1.5 billion, this figure is highly preliminary and subject to change as the design evolves. Given its massive scale, constructing MIRA on a 50-acre site at Brookhaven National Laboratory in New York seems like a logical choice. Although the time frame for completion is uncertain, scientists believe construction could take around a decade followed by several more decades of operation. Despite the challenges and uncertainties surrounding funding and site selection, the potential of MIRA to drive groundbreaking research, inspire innovation, and contribute significantly to humanity makes this project an exciting and worthwhile venture. The initial design and conceptual phase is estimated to cost around $20 million and could be completed within three to four years. To move forward, MIRA needs funding, a designated site, and a strong, collaborative research team. This growth graph is essentially a projection of the triangulation space $T_d$ for a given dimension $d$, and as such, it offers a more accessible framework for examining the properties of triangulations compared to the conventional metric structure defined by the fabric space. In particular, this new perspective becomes particularly useful for exploring the limits of finite-scale truncations of the triangulation space, allowing us to establish a key result: for any given shape dimension $d$, there exists a finite scaling parameter $k_d$ such that for $k_d$ or larger, the corresponding shapes have dimensions greater than $d$. We have further analyzed the relationship between $k_d$ and $d$, finding that $k_d$ increases proportionally to the square root of $d$, i.e., $k_d \approx 2.75\sqrt{d}$. This result provides a novel insight into the fundamental properties of shapes and their corresponding dimensions within the context of triangulations. Additionally, we have an associated conjecture proposing that the distribution of shape dimensions undergo a transition from a Gaussian distribution to a power law distribution with a crossover point related to the square of the mean shape dimension. To validate or refute this conjecture, we have an analytical approach based on the projected growth graph, offering a quantitative characterization of this transition and the associated crossover scale. This characterization is expressed in terms of the specific shape distribution parameters and can be tested through simulations of random triangulations. It has also led to the development of an analytical approach for studying the properties of random surfaces, which can be applied to other research scenarios. Initially, we consider single Higgs production and Higgs pair creation at these colliders, focusing on the impact of BSM physics on these processes and providing effective field theory descriptions. Subsequently, we explore the responsiveness of these processes to BSM Higgs interactions at various TeV energy levels, and conclude that double Higgs creation stands out as particularly sensitive to such interactions, given its already significant cross-section at 100 GeV energy colliders. Moreover, we find that this process exhibits a distinctive topological characteristic, namely the presence of a hadronic jet triple system, which arises as a result of the massive nature of heavy Higgs bosons and their decay products. Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on accurate non-rigid registration between 3D volumes and 3D surface models, especially in neurosurgery. Although deep learning-based methods have achieved significant performance, their effectiveness is limited by the availability of training data, which is often a critical issue in clinical settings. In contrast, biomechanical models offer a promising alternative, but their slow computation and difficulty in parameter selection make them less practical for real-time applications. We present a novel biMechanical Volume-to-Surface Alignment Framework (BVS-AF) that combines the strengths of both approaches. A fast and numerically stable finite element method is used to obtain an initial alignment, from which a robust and efficient feature extraction technique is derived to enhance the alignment using minimal adjustment. This efficient process allows for real-time adaptation of the model to new data, without re-estimating time-consuming material parameters. We validate BVS-AF on a publicly available dataset, showing its efficacy and comparing its performance to state-of-the-art deep learning-based methods on a privately collected dataset of 30 brain volumes.
