Acquiring large datasets for training models is a significant hurdle in machine learning applications, particularly for challenging tasks like scene flow estimation. This paper introduces an innovative Adversarial Metric Learning (AML) framework to address this issue in self-taught learning settings. Within AML, two novel components are presented: a metric learning technique and a minimax optimization approach. These components work in tandem to create a robust self-taught learning method that leverages limited supervised data and utilizes abundant, unsupervised neighbor relationships found in target images. The proposed framework ensures that the model generalizes effectively on new data by minimizing the discrepancy between the learned and actual neighbor distances. This is achieved through a critical threshold that defines a temporal correspondence mask, thereby enabling the model to differentiate between corresponding points on the scene flow map. The effectiveness of AML is demonstrated through scene flow estimation experiments, using both synthetic and real-world datasets, and comparing it favorably to state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, a case study is presented, showcasing how AML can be applied to estimate scene flows from monocular images. The proposed method's source code is available at https://github.com/lingyu-gh/AMLFLOW. The code has also been successfully utilized to estimate scene flows from real-world images captured by a single RGBD camera. The resulting dataset, named RGBDFLOW, comprises 5000 densely labeled 3D flow maps, alongside the corresponding 3D point clouds and RGB images, and is available for public use at https://github.com/lingyu-gh/RGBDFLOW. The proposed method has also been evaluated on the SIFTFlow and RFM Datasets, yielding outstanding performance results. The proposed AML framework provides novel insights into metric learning, deriving a continuous quality score for correspondences based on the Nearest Neighbor Contrastive (NNC) loss, and demonstrating the effectiveness of NNC for evaluating the quality of correspondences, even when the target distribution is unknown. The challenges of scene flow estimation, monitored through qualitative and quantitative performance metrics, include flow occlusion, noisy correspondences, and dense depth estimation. The proposed method has addressed these challenges by introducing continuous quality scores for correspondences, leveraging abundant unsampled neighbor relationships on the target distribution, and combining the AML with a fully connected dense depth estimator, resulting in an innovative self-taught learning framework, and providing rigorous evaluations through numerous challenging experiments. The proposed method has also been applied to estimate scene flows from monocular images, demonstrating the versatility and generality of AML

This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-aligned strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at high temperatures, using a mean field approach. We then used the Bayesian framework to make predictions about the structure of quark stars in various scenarios. The study shows that a spin-aligned quark star's structure is significantly affected by an inclined magnetic field, particularly at low temperatures. Furthermore, we found that the Bayesian evidence favors the assumption that the quark matter's density is non-uniform in magnetic fields, rather than the commonly held belief in uniform density. This study also clarifies the conditions under which the spin-aligned star and the conventional strange quark star coexist. We derived these conditions using the Bayesian framework and found that in a wide range of scenarios, the spin-aligned star and the conventional strange quark star do not have distinct max mass values. Instead, we found that there is a gradual transition from the spin-aligned state to the conventional state as the star's mass increases. Additionally, we found that the spin-aligned state and the conventional state can coexist within a certain temperature range. This study also analyzed the effects of different particle interactions on the quark star's structure and found that the particle interactions that contribute positively to the pressure increase the star's mass, while the negative contributions lead to a decrease in the mass. A designated pairing function among the vertices of a simple graph turns it into a structured model, known as a semi-eulerian graph, with specific properties including an even number of paired vertices. This study defines two distinct types of structured models: those with no unpaired vertices (eulerian graphs) and those with paired and unpaired vertices (semi-eulerian graphs). A key contribution of this work is to demonstrate the equivalence between two distinct concepts: the pairing function of a semi-eulerian graph and a particular type of hamiltonian circuit through its vertices. Additionally, an edge-tinting operation is introduced and proven to preserve the property of being a semi-eulerian graph. A notable result arising from this property is the relationship between a hamiltonian circuit and the pairing function of a semi-eulerian graph constructed from it. A further finding shows that not all semi-eulerian graphs can be generated from a hamiltonian circuit, demonstrating this relationship does not hold as a universal principle. A previously known requirement for a graph to be eulerian is shown to be equivalent to the condition that all its pairing functions are harmonic, with harmonic defined as a property that is preserved under edge-tinting. A new characterization of a graph as eulerian is presented, based on the harmony of its pairing functions, and a construction method is also provided. A specifically analyzed cubic graph in this study is found to have a particular pairing function harmony, with implications for a related hamiltonian circuit. A further investigation into this circuit's subpaths and their relationships with the graph's edges and vertices uncovers another harmonic property. A generalization of this property is then proven to be true for all cubic graphs. A particular edge-tinting operation is introduced and its effect on a graph's pairing functions and hamiltonian circuits is explored, with a resulting conclusion about the impossibility of certain harmonic pairings on a specific class of cubic graphs. A direct conversion method is provided for a hamiltonian circuit from a related dual graph, with an additional observation about the preservation of harmonic pairings under this conversion. A further investigation into the structure of the original graph based on its dual graph and a related hamiltonian circuit leads to another possible construction method for the original graph, with an associated condition that the pairing functions must be harmonic. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for creating personalized system call filters for virtualized microservices. When operating in a cloud environment, microservices within a Docker container can be isolated from each other using system call rules, which can, however, slow down the microservices through unnecessary overhead. To optimize this, we propose the Timeloops approach, featuring an automated learning phase and a policy evaluation phase. During the learning phase, Timeloops generates a temporary virtual environment where it observes the behavior of each microservice and creates a initial guess for the system call filters. In the evaluation phase, the approach simulates the timeline of each microservice, compares it with the predicted behavior, and based on the results, it either confirms the initial guess or suggests a rule to block specific system calls. We tested the Timeloops approach on real-world datasets consisting of various containers and found that it reduces the overhead of system call filtering by approximately 70% while achieving a nearly 100% accuracy rate. Furthermore, the results showed that the approach outperforms the existing state-of-the-art method called CCFinder in terms of both efficiency and effectiveness. The proposed method has a user-friendly command-line interface that is optimized for Linux-based operating systems. The code for the Timeloops approach, along with the related datasets and evaluation results, is available for public access on GitHub. The proposed method has the potential to be an highly efficient tool for creating personalized system call filters for virtualized microservices, making it an valuable contribution to the field. A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear migration occurs. While this process has been observed across many organisms, only a few studies have examined the underlying mechanisms in any depth. Through the use of high-speed light microscopy and quantitative analysis, we have investigated interkinetic nuclear movement in the developing zebrafish retina. Our findings reveal that dispersion plays a key role in the generation of retinal layer patterns through the distribution of cell nuclei during development. As a result, the distribution of nuclei can be seen as following a Gaussian pattern, with the degree of spread directly influencing their layering. We have also observed that the direction of movement reverses in certain areas of the retina, which results in the formation of sharp gradients in layering, primarily observed where the retina's widest and thinnest layers meet. Conversely, any sudden changes in layering patterns are thought to arise from changes in the direction of movement rather than migration speeds. Notably, our research demonstrates that the term "directional wave" previously used to describe interkinetic nuclear movement may no longer be accurate, and instead suggests that migration patterns could be better understood through the study of neurons at a more individual level. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the concept of wave-like movement overestimates the scale of retinal layer patterning formation, with any dispersion accounted for being significantly less than previous estimates. Nonetheless, our findings do support the role of synchronized movement in pattern formation, and also reveal that the layering patterns themselves can be altered through changes in the direction of movement rather than migration speeds. In addition, our research demonstrates that the development of the retina's widest and thinnest layers is driven by distinct cellular processes, which differ between these two layers. The YORP effect exerts a gentle influence on asteroids' rotation by generating a torque that is directly proportional to the square of the solar flux and the square of the eccentricity of their orbits. As such, it tends to drive faster rotation among asteroids in the inner solar system. A neural network implementation is proposed that uses complex weights to efficiently simulate a variety of one-dimensional models, including the one-dimensional Hubbard model. This approach simplifies the network architecture, eliminating the need for unitary parameter transformations, and significantly speeds up computation by reducing the number of complex multiplications required. A key benefit of this method is that it naturally avoids the Hubbard Sign Dilemma, a challenge faced by traditional real-weight neural networks due to the complex phase of the wave functions. This issue arises because traditional networks struggle to learn the absolute values and phases of the wave functions separately, leading to the Signs Dilemma. Despite only using a single complex-valued network, the proposed approach allows for accurate phase and density predictions with real-weight network duplicates. This method's efficiency and density/phase prediction accuracy are demonstrated through simulations of a one-dimensional Hubbard model using both periodic and open boundary conditions. Furthermore, this model's ability to learn site-to-site phase correlations is utilized to implement a simple, accurate finite-size correction formula for density predictions. This analysis shows that this complex network effectively addresses the Signs Dilemma and provides accurate results for finite-size densities, offering a precise correction and confirming the predictive capability of the model. Additionally, this method's predictive capability is applied to learn wave function phases in a simple double-donor model, thereby validating the proposed approach's validity and utility. This research paves the way for a range of applications, including the efficient simulation of models experiencing the Signs Dilemma, the development of complex neural operators, and the validation of theoretical predictions of wave function phase learning, given its findings based on numerical simulations. This work is also relevant to a broader range of models and offers guidance on a range of research questions, as well as providing raw data for further analysis. This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides an overview of the complex neural network used in this research, Section 3 discusses its application to the Hubbard model, Section 4 examines this model's ability to learn finite-size correction formulas, Section 5 explores its prediction capabilities in a double-donor model, and in Section 6 the proposed approach is compared to alternative methods used to simulate the Hubbard model. We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-based method known as ReCross, which employs prior experiences to augment the model's training data without requiring explicit instructions.
This method employs a rich library of labeled examples derived from completed tasks, allowing the model to refine its understanding and expand its knowledge in an unsupervised manner.
To effectively deploy ReCross, we introduce a plain text precursor called the Data Footprint, which serves as a concise summary of the underlying data and facilitates high-quality retrievals.
Through extensive experiments on both text-to-text and classification tasks, ReCross demonstrates consistent and substantial improvements in unsupervised cross-task generalization, outperforming multiple baselines and alternative methods in various settings. This approach's versatility is further illustrated by its applicability to both T0 and FLAN, as well as other comparable models. The resulting code has been publicly disseminated on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/ReCross. This study's findings have significant implications for the development of multiple-niche models, showcasing the potential of targeted, unsupervised adaptation to enhance performance in specific domains. This research has also identified several engaging future challenges, including the integration of ReCross with explicit cross-task guidance and the development of a more sophisticated Data Footprint Extraction method. This approach's results have been further validated through a rigorous evaluation across multiple diverse datasets, yielding consistent and quantifiable gains in unsupervised cross-task generalization. A boolean structure on a group G is defined as a function f: G → G with specific properties, and it is proven that any group with a boolean operation is essentially a group with a specific type of automorphism, known as an inversion that preserves order and has a 2-cycle effect. This results in the development of a precise criterion for a group to be abelian, as well as generalizations to groups that operate under different principles, such as the fundamental group of a hyperbolic surface. Additionally, a connection is established between boolean structures and specific types of permutations, known as involutions, that can be arranged in a sequence. This connection is utilized in proving that any group that is generated by a finite set of involutions that follow a specific pattern is essentially a group that is generated by a minimal set of those involutions. This particular result can be applied to a broad range of groups, including Coxeter groups, finite groups, and the fundamental group of a hyperbolic surface. It is also proven that groups that are generated by a finite set of involutions that follow a specific pattern have a specific properties known as the faithfulness property, which means that any representation of the group can be visualized as a particular type of permutation that is generated by those involutions. This result is further generalized to groups that operate under different principles, such as the fundamental group of a hyperbolic surface, and even leads to a generalization of the faithfulness property known as the strong faithfulness property. This latter property is proven to be equivalent to the group being generated by a finite set of involutions that follow a specific pattern, and it provides a solution to a previously unresolved problem that was posed by the second author. It is also shown that the faithfulness property is not preserved when the group in question is changed from a finite group to the fundamental group of a hyperbolic surface, and this results in the development of two new surfaces whose fundamental groups have the faithfulness property, as well as provide a negative answer to yet another problem that was posed by the second author. The COVID-19 pandemic spread rapidly globally in early 2020, causing severe consequences in China, especially in Wuhan. In this environment, digital rumors about the virus gained significant traction on social media platforms in China. Our analysis of 1,565 identified rumors focuses on exploring spread patterns, false information types, and the impact of truth-seeking efforts on dissemination and credibility. Our study reveals that the most widely spread rumors often incorporated partial truth, accounted for 26.48% of all rumors, and that the majority of rumors tended to target specific groups. Our analysis also found that credible sources were effective in quelling the spread of rumors but that some persisted due to emotional resonance with users. Ultimately, our research found that platform administrators' efforts to curb spreading rumors were successful but that some persistent rumors continued to circulate despite these efforts. Our study provides insights into the mechanisms underlying the spread of digital rumors and offers policy recommendations to enhance crisis management through targeted measures to address source trust, user psychology, and platform governance. Our research can be applied to understanding and managing similar situations in other countries and elsewhere in China. Integrating continuous queries into streams with unknown data patterns provides maximum flexibility, yet processing such streams poses a challenge due to unpredictable stream rates. Existing solutions, focusing primarily on large datasets, often overlook efficiency in dynamic settings. In response, we present a novel approach, called LifeFlow, a stream processing engine designed to handle streams with varying data frequencies. To accommodate different data arrival patterns, LifeFlow employs multiple processing pathways for each query, tailoring execution rates to match varying input spectra. Furthermore, to ensure scalability and performance, LifeFlow utilizes a distributed architecture, dividing each query pathway into multiple modules executed across a network of processing nodes. To demonstrate LifeFlow's superiority, we compared its performance with that of a highly optimized batch processing engine and a leading stream processing system, showcasing LifeFlow's efficiency in processing large, intricate datasets and streams with complex query workflows. In assessment trials, LifeFlow processed streams of up to 10 times length than Apache Flink, with query execution rates on par with those of a highly optimized batch engine. In addition, LifeFlow outperformed Flink in both processing time and memory usage in tests of complex queries and large datasets streams. In further analysis, LifeFlow's performance was found to be particularly effective when evaluating time-changing frequency streams, improving processing speeds by as much as 87% over Flink. In conclusion, LifeFlow's innovative approach and efficient architecture make it an exceptionally versatile and highly efficient stream processing engine, suitable for a broad range of real-world applications. In particular, LifeFlow excels in situations involving varying data frequencies, complex queries, and limited computational resources, as seen in experiments with rolling window streams, Flink, and Apache Spark. In these contexts, LifeFlow's performance outperformed that of both Flink and Spark, with processing speed improvements of up to 700% over Flink and 15% over Spark. In response to performance limitations observed with certain large dataset streams, LifeFlow was modified to include a new optimization feature, known as "Tuning Flow," that further enhances performance by adjusting engine parameters automatically. In further testing, the enhanced version, with Tunning Flow, processed certain large dataset streams with complex query workflows over 3 times length than the original LifeFlow engine. This study investigates how the loss function functions, particularly the chosen loss function's structure and its optimal hyperparameters, affect the model's efficacy. We focus on a fundamental loss function, the multinomial loss function, and explore two key loss function alterations: modifying the loss function's structure by adding a regularization term, and deviating from the optimal hyperparameters. We develop a theoretical framework to analyze these changes' effects on the model's performance. Our theoretical findings reveal that both loss function alterations result in a decrease in performance, as measured by the test set loss or the confusion matrix. We validate our proposed framework through extensive experiments using MNIST, CIFAR10, and ResNet on the ImageNet dataset. Our results support our theoretical predictions, demonstrating that both loss function alterations lead to suboptimal performance. We also observe that restoring the chosen loss function to its original form, without any regularization or using the optimal hyperparameters, is essential to achieving the best results. Our study's implications for deep learning practitioners are clear: to excel at classification tasks, it is essential to use the Kullback-Leibler divergence-based loss function, which is the natural choice, without any additional regularization. We emphasize that using an inappropriate loss function, even if it is a sophisticated one, will always lead to subpar results. Our proposed framework provides a blueprint for investigating other loss function alterations, thereby offering a valuable tool for the deep learning community. We conclude by highlighting some promising research directions, including analyzing how to design more effective loss function structures and delving into the relationship between loss function alterations and adversarial attacks. Our study's findings are relevant to a broad range of applications that involve predicting categorical outcomes, including computer vision, natural language processing, and recommender systems. Our proposed framework can be applied to these domains by simply redefining the loss function alterations and model efficacy metrics. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis. The importance of correctly classifying the type of superconducting order parameter is also discussed, with recommendations to use the sum rule of the $f$-sum rule to determine the correct value of magnetic susceptibility. A discussion on the possible locations of the Fermi surface and its impact on magnetic susceptibility is also given, along with a focused examination of the effects of electron-electron interaction on the order parameter in a specific orientation of the Fermi surface. The possible occurrence of a singular response to an applied magnetic field in a particular orientation of the Fermi surface is proposed as the underlying cause for the observed complexity of the specific heat curve in experimental data. The results of this analysis are summarized in a set of equations that can be directly compared with existing experimental and theoretical data on the subject. The possible occurrences of and differences between the responses of chiral and nematic superconducting states to an applied magnetic field and the effects of electron-electron interaction on these responses are also discussed in this summary. The results of this analysis are also reflected in a set of figures that illustrate and confirm the complexity of the specific heat curve and the singular response to an applied magnetic field in a particular orientation of the Fermi surface. This paper investigates the conditions under which traditional coherent CPM detection is inferior to non-coherent differential CPM detection, with the aim of identifying scenarios where non-coherent differential detection outperforms its coherent counterpart. The key requirement for non-coherent differential detection to excel is that the symbol duration must significantly surpass a particular threshold, which is determined to be approximately 2.5 times the duration needed for a sinusoidal pulse of the same bandwidth as the CPM signal. The paper further analyzes non-coherent detection performance and finds that, in general, CPM with a BPSK differential baseband signal will have the best performance, followed by QPSK and octal phase-shift keying (OPSKK), with MSK and GMSK having similar performance. In addition, the findings are validated through an extensive Monte-Carlo simulation study. The research also derives an upper bound on the required delay threshold and demonstrates that, for any given CPM scheme, there exists a certain SNRD threshold such that, when the required delay exceeds this threshold, non-coherent differential detection will always be more robust than coherent detection below that SNRD threshold. The paper further delves into an analytical assessment of several well-known CPM schemes, including BPSK, QPSK, OPSKK, MSK, GMSK, and minisequence based CPM, and obtains numerical values for their respective delay thresholds. The results obtained through simulation confirm that, when the required delay exceeds the derived threshold, non-coherent differential detection will always provide a robustness advantage over coherent detection. The research also explores various pulse shaping options for minisequence based CPM and finds that some of these options may not necessarily provide a performance advantage over coherent detection. The paper concludes by investigating several commonly used pulse shapes, including both symmetric and asymmetric shapes, and finds that only certain shapes, such as the raised cosine and root raised cosine shapes, provide a performance advantage over coherent detection when the required delay exceeds a certain threshold. The research further analyzes the impact of changing the roll-off factor on the required delay threshold and finds that, for a given level of robustness, there is a minimum level of average signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) needed to provide that level of robustness, and that this required level of average SNR increases as the roll-off factor of the pulse shape decreases. The results obtained through simulation confirm that, for a given level of robustness, the required delay must exceed a certain threshold that increases with the desired level of average SNR

In this paper, the quantum potential is analyzed in the context of a massless scalar field, both in 2D and 4D quantum field theory. The quantum field theory framework is applied to a scalar field with a $\phi^3$ self-interaction in 2D and $\phi^4$ in 4D. The purpose of examining these self-interacting scenarios is to investigate the relationship between the quantum field's mean squared value and its energy-momentum tensor. The compressibility of spacetime's vacuum is then calculated as the negative derivative of the mean squared value of the scalar field with respect to its energy-momentum tensor. The results indicate that the spacetime's vacuum compressibility is negative one unit of order, equivalent to one in 2D and unity in 4D, despite variations in temperature, due to the nature of the self-interacting field. The possibility of such a transition is supported by the results obtained from numerical simulations, which display the compressibility of the vacuum changing sign as the self-coupling parameter increases. Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday common knowledge facts represented as if-then statements, which we assemble from a diverse range of sources including user interactions, text, and videos.  This comprehensive set of normal everyday common knowledge facts is novel in its scope and scale, and we believe it offers significant value to the artificial intelligence community by providing a large amount of data with complex structure that is challenging to model, and a wide range of tasks to demonstrate the utility of the data, from developing more sophisticated inference algorithms to creating more realistic and engaging interactive virtual worlds.  With over 150,000 recorded premises and conclusions from diverse sources, and a sophisticated taxonomy that captures the underlying context and underlying assumptions of each conclusion, ATOMIC presents a unique challenge and opportunity for the community, and we make this dataset available to the public for the advancement of artificial intelligence.

In pursuit of a functional quantum annealer, researchers can leverage asset allocation techniques to get the most out of their resources. Literature on this subject primarily focuses on classical settings, with some basic quantum considerations. However, there's a lack of research addressing the challenges posed by noise and limited qubits in actual quantum devices. This study fills this gap by introducing a new method, Quantum Hybrid HHL, which combines classical and quantum HHL implementations to accommodate the constraints of real-world quantum machines. Quantum Hybrid HHL assets a hybrid approach that utilizes classical assets for the most challenging components, such as recombining amplitudes, while keeping classical resources minimal. The research also involves developing an efficient implementation of recombination circuits and new asset allocation objectives that mitigate amplitude recombination's difficulties. When applied to real annealer data, this study's findings yield successful recombination circuits that outperform conventional classical methods by an order of magnitude in terms of resource utilization. Moreover, this research offers a practical solution for tackling large-scale matrix inversion problems within the constraints of current quantum devices, with real-world applications such as portfolio optimization demonstrated on a 32-qubit annealer. The code developed as part of this research has been made publicly available on GitHub. The study also involves an experimental investigation of quantum hybrid HHL's scalability, which reveals that despite the advent of next-generation quantum machines, the challenges posed by noise and limited qubits will continue to hinder the efficiency of asset allocation in the near future. To further improve listening alone under limited-labelling situations, we propose a new multimodal training approach for enhanced speech recognition. This method involves training both transcribers and encoders/decoders on the same data, initially transcribing speech and subsequently encoding the transcription. To prevent feedback loops during decoding, we only use the initial transcription. As the system learns from both forward and reverse tasks, we term it bidirectional. To prevent overwhelming of the encoder by the decoder, we implemented a focus mechanism on the encoder, prioritizing hidden states that differ between the forward and reverse tasks. With these innovations, we successfully improved the speech recognition accuracy. To validate our proposed method, we conducted extensive experiments using both ResNet and Conformer structures for encoders and decoders. Our results showed that the proposed bidirectional focus method delivers superior results over conventional speech-text driven training, with the CER rate decreasing by 8.5% for ResNet and 12.8% for Conformer on the Librispeech dataset. Our proposed approach is also compatible with other speech-text driven training methods, enabling straightforward integration into existing multimodal training systems. Moreover, our analysis revealed that the focus mechanism is an effective means of reducing the impact of decoder feedback on the encoder, and that both forward and reverse tasks are necessary for achieving optimal performance. To facilitate reproducibility, we made our code available online. With further exploration, our results suggest that the focus mechanism delivers superior results over random initial transcriptions, whereas the bidirectional focus leads to inferior results without the focus mechanism. To optimize our approach for limited labelled data, we proposed a simpler version of the bidirectional focus method, replacing the encoder with a teacher that uses the same data as the student. Our experiments confirmed the effectiveness of this simpler version on both the Librispeech and VCTK datasets, with the CER rate decreasing by 13.6% and 19.4% respectively. Our proposed approach provides a scalable, high-performance baseline for enhanced speech recognition, surpassing the state-of-the-art results achieved using semi-supervised learning without the need for additional labelled data. This article uses combinatorial and analytic methods to analyze the set of natural numbers represented by the sum of their digits in base $k$, added to their largest significant digit minus one, where this conversion is considered for a variable base $k$. Initially, we established an analogy between these numbers and the integer partitions mentioned in the Allsorts paper, where it is shown that the generating functions for the number of integer partitions with specific properties can be derived from the basic partition generating function through the application of combinatorial operators. Now, in this current work, we will utilize this analogy to investigate the structure of the numbers that result from this conversion process in base $k$, with a particular focus on the asymptotic behavior of these numbers as they appear in the context of uniform parking functions. A key contribution of this paper is to demonstrate that the numbers obtained from this conversion process are statistically indistinguishable from the numbers obtained by randomly selecting a $k$-digit number and then adding up its digits, where $k$ is a parameter that determines both the base of the number system and the degree of the polynomial used in this calculation. As a result, we are able to derive an explicit expression for the mean of these numbers, and also establish that their distribution is narrowly concentrated around this mean value with a quadratic growth rate. A further analysis of these numbers in the context of uniform parking functions also reveals a critical property: the minimum possible value of these numbers in any given base $k$ is equal to $k$, and all the bases $k$ that are less than a certain threshold ($8.32\ldots$) include numbers with the property of being maximal, where a number is considered maximal if it cannot be increased by a single-unit change in any of its digits. Measurements of superconducting nanowires can reveal the existence of coherent quantum phases, but have also been misinterpreted in the past as evidence for Coulomb blockade. We distinguish between these phenomena by demonstrating the precise control of ionization events in Ti and gate-regulated classical Coulomb jumps in NbN nanowires, unaffected by phase fluctuations. This achievement allows us to focus on the quantum aspects and observe the characteristic N-shape in $dV_d/dV_g$, a marker of Shottky gap renormalization, which signals the onset of Josephson current. Furthermore, we exploit the versatility of our setup to explore the intricate relationship between the Josephson current, Coulomb jumps, and phase fluctuations in the nanowires. Our findings also highlight the distinct behaviors exhibited by Ti nanowires, showcasing persistent Joule heating effects and phase-jump sequences reminiscent of classical Scarring States. Our approach involves measuring the $I$-$V$ characteristics of the nanowires using a low-frequency lock-in technique and a custom-built measurement platform that enables rapid adjustment of all relevant control parameters. By combining and analyzing multiple data sets obtained through various measurements, including lock-in, capacitance, and ionization event spectra, we have gained a comprehensive understanding of the nanowires' quantum and classical dynamics. Our study has implications for the utilization of nanowires in quantum information processing and provides a cautionary tale about the potential for misinterpretation of measurement data. Our results also demonstrate the versatility of Ti nanowires, which exhibit unique properties that set them apart from other superconducting materials. Our findings have been theoretically validated through simulations of the nanowires' dynamics, which have helped us navigate the complex interplay between the nanowires' quantum, thermal, and geometric attributes. Our approach has resulted in a comprehensive and quantitative description of the nanowires' behavior, which has paved the way for the development of theoretical models that can predict their dynamics in complex scenarios. Our study has further led to the discovery of two previously unknown phenomena: Quantum Scarring States and Phase-Jump Sequences, which have been observed in Ti nanowires and can potentially be utilized for the development of quantum information processing and other technological applications. Our research has also resulted in the creation of a comprehensive and open-source code called TiNano, which is capable of simulating the dynamics of Ti nanowires and has been used to validate our measurement data and provide a theoretical understanding of the nanowires' behavior. Our findings have been presented at international conferences

Understanding how epidemics spread within densely populated environments like urban public transportation systems is crucial for developing effective public health strategies. Epidemic models set on a bus network can result in conflicting outcomes, making it difficult to predict whether an introduced pathogen will rapidly spread throughout the community or remain contained. To address this challenge, we are using a simple model that simulates the introduction of a pathogen into a bus network and analyzing its behavior to better grasp the underlying dynamics. By incorporating a variety of factors, including different routing methods, we are identifying the conditions under which a pathogen is likely to spread extensively. Our research involves analyzing a simple model that simulates the introduction of a pathogen into a bus network and examining its behavior to better understand the underlying dynamics. We are exploring the connection between this model and another, more complex model that represents the bus network as a whole, and investigating how different routing methods affect the model's stability. Our primary goal is to determine the conditions under which a pathogen will spread rapidly throughout the community or remain contained. Our findings suggest that overestimating the degree to which passengers on different buses interact with one another can actually contribute to the spread of a pathogen, while underestimating these interactions may result in the introduction of a highly contagious pathogen being initially contained. Our research also implies that the model's stability is influenced by the routing methods used, with some methods leading to the spread of a pathogen more efficiently than others. Our study demonstrates that a carefully designed bus network can significantly reduce the spread of a pathogen, and that overestimating the interactions between passengers on different buses can contribute to the spread of a pathogen, while underestimating these interactions may result in the introduction of a highly contagious pathogen being initially contained. Our results also show that the model's stability is influenced by the routing methods used, with some methods leading to the spread of a pathogen more efficiently than others. Our findings have implications for various other complex systems that involve densely connected components, and our research provides a useful model for examining the dynamics of these systems. Our study set on an urban bus network demonstrates that overestimating the interactions between components can lead to the spread of a pathogen more efficiently than underestimating these interactions, and that the design of these components, in this case the bus network, can also affect the dynamics of the system. The GMR effect in a 20nm thick Bi/Co multilayer stack has been investigated by GMR and AHE measurements. Due to its large thickness, the spin-orbit proximity effect is significant, likely caused by bulk scattering. A model was developed to explain the reduced magnitude of the AHE compared to the GMR effect, considering the angle of scattering and the spin-orbit proximity effect. It was found that the AHE resistance approached the GMR resistance as the scattering angle increased, indicating that the spin-orbit proximity effect's influence on the AHE was minimal. It was also discovered that the spin-orbit proximity effect's impact could be negligible in thinner multilayer stacks with similar thicknesses. The results demonstrate that the spin-orbit proximity effect alone cannot fully account for the reduced AHE magnitude, suggesting that other factors such as interface scattering also play a crucial role. The lack of influence of the spin-orbit proximity effect on the AHE in thinner stacks aligns with previous research findings. The study's results were validated through comparison with previous Bi/Co GMR research, revealing that the AHE resistance was over two times the GMR resistance in thinner stacks with smaller scattering lengths. Our key finding shows that imposing this constraint is equivalent to a weighted $l_2$ regularization on the network's parameters. Our proposed method, which applies this concept to multi-layer networks, results in improved performance in various benchmark settings. Our approach can be integrated into existing networks with minimal modifications, and we provide a straightforward implementation of Lipschitz regularizer that is computationally efficient. To achieve this, we are developing a robust neural network that can effectively utilize both PET and CT images acquired at different dose levels. This network should be capable of accurately segmenting tissue and reconstructing low-dose PET images, even when CT images are obtained at a higher dose than typically encountered in clinical settings. To ensure reliability, it's crucial that the network can successfully operate in a variety of scenarios involving different dose combinations, including out-of-distribution data that might arise in real-world applications. To train and validate this network, we are utilizing a custom dataset composed of PET and CT images acquired at varying dose levels, with a focus on both normal and abnormal tissue samples. This paper investigates the link between CT and modern Coreference Resolution systems using Artificial Neural Networks to understand if such systems are influenced by the principles of CT or if they can achieve similar results on own accord. To this end, we examined the relationship between CT-defined centers and f-cores with a large, annotated dataset for coreference. Our analysis shows that the two are highly similar, indicating that the systems themselves can account for this coherence without external guidance. To validate our findings, we proposed and implemented two simple experiments that involve either limiting the ability of systems to find centers or by manipulating the way centers are defined to coerce the systems into mimicking the behavior described by CT. Our results confirm our initial observations and provide a framework for exploring the relationships between coherence, coreference, and the structure of sentences. This framework has utility for conducting similar analyses on other datasets and other research related to the coherence of conversations. The beam-charge bunching technique used in Energy Recovery Linacs (ERLs) produces beam-charge fluctuations that cause beam loss due to beam-Beam Interactions (BBIs).  To evaluate loss generation, the beam loss probability function is calculated using the beam-Beam effect's fluctuation impact.  Initially, studies focused primarily on the effects of beam loss probability caused by beam-Beam interactions in the ring.  However, it has been found that beam loss probability is influenced by the filling configuration, specifically the number of bunches and the beam separation.  This study examines the relationship between the filling configuration and beam loss probability.  As beam separation increases, the probability of loss diminishes exponentially with a characteristic length of approximately 10-20 meters.  Furthermore, the probability of loss at the beginning of a batch is found to be directly proportional to the number of bunches.  To prevent excessive ring loss, a more substantial initial batch is recommended in designs similar to the Compact X-Band ERL.  Additionally, the probability of loss increases exponentially with the length of a batch, suggesting that shorter batches are preferable.  The dominant loss generation mechanism shifts from beam-Beam interactions at the beginning of a batch to beam fragmentation instability towards the end of a batch.  The ring's stability to beam fragmentation instability was found to be sensitive to the filling configuration, with the optimal configuration dependent on the ring's characteristics.  The ring's stability to beam fragmentation instability can be influenced by changing the beam separation within a batch, which may allow for larger batches with minimal increase in loss generation.  The optimal filling configuration varies across different ring designs but must prioritize shorter batches and adequate beam separation to prevent excessive loss generation induced by beam fragmentation instability.  The ring's stability to beam fragmentation instability can be evaluated using the ring's shunt impedance, with a general guideline being that the ring's stability to beam fragmentation instability is sufficient if the ring's shunt impedance is less than approximately 50 kΩ.  The impact of the filling configuration on beam loss probability is expected to vary across different ring designs but must be evaluated on a case-by-case basis to ensure reliable and stable ERL operation.  The ring's stability to beam fragmentation instability can also be influenced by changing the beam charge, which may allow for larger charges with minimal increase in loss generation.  The optimal filling configuration and beam charge vary across different ring designs but must prioritize shorter batches, adequate beam separation, and sufficient shunt impedance to prevent excessive loss generation induced by beam fragmentation instability

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. In this work, the dispersive part of a one-loop six-gluon amplitude in N=4 SYM theory was calculated under a NMRK kinematic limit and shown to be composed of a two-gluon CEV, allowing extraction of the latter for all helicity configurations. Although this calculation was constrained to the NMRK limit, the resulting two-gluon CEV exhibits significant complexity in both color and kinematic dependence, mirroring characteristics found in general six-gluon amplitude configurations. In such scenarios, six-gluon amplitude functions can be expressed using impact factors, trajectories, CEVs for single-emission processes, and a residual component defined by conformally invariant cross ratios that characterise six-gluon amplitudes in N=4 SYM theory. As expected, under a stricter MRK kinematic limit, the two-gluon CEV can be decomposed into a product of two single-emission CEVs. In both limits, the two-gluon CEV exhibits significant symmetry properties, specifically under exchange of the two most widely spaced gluons and under T-duality. These properties are consistent with predictions made by maximally-helicity-violating (MHV) vertex hypotheses proposed in the context of N=4 SYM theory. Nonetheless, beneath its symmetric and T-dual invariant appearance, the two-gluon CEV reveals a complex interior that cannot be accounted for by these hypotheses. The metric dimension of a graph G, denoted by md(G), represents the minimum number of vertices in a subset W of G's vertices, so that any pair of distinct vertices in G can be distinguished by their unique nearest neighbor to the vertices in W. Here we discuss shortened versions of this concept, proposing the minimum number n (less than md(G)) that allows distinct vertex pairs to be distinguished as good approximation dimension (AAD(n,G)) and similar variants. These new definitions can be viewed as intermediate measures between the number of vertices in a minimal identifying set (minID(G)) and the metric dimension of a graph. We also examine the relationship between these new dimensions and established metrics, as well as specific instances related to localized versions of these new dimensions. Furthermore, we establish lower and upper bounds for the AAD(n,G) and provide a precise value for a particular tree structure. Additionally, we offer an alternative formulation for the minID(G) and demonstrate its application in determining the minimum identifying set for a given vertex, which can differ from the set defined by the metric dimension. Lastly, we conclude by outlining potential future research avenues related to these new dimensions.

Researchers employed a neural network to refine all-sky maps created by the Fermi Large Area Telescope, considering various source models. A convolutional neural network was used to create a refined map, demonstrating significant improvements in background subtraction, particularly in heavily saturated regions. To account for variable sources, a recurrent neural network was employed, successfully recovering known source spectra and light curves, even for sources exhibiting complex patterns of activity. This work paves the way for utilizing neural networks for large datasets and complex data analysis problems, and provides refined maps and source profiles suitable for study. Moreover, this method demonstrates potential utility for identifying anomalous sources, and we highlight such sources exhibiting irregular patterns of activity, including a super-Orion CLUMPS giant molecular cloud complex, previously unreported as variable, along with several active galactic nuclei showing broad spectral variations, and a star formation region exhibiting temporal and spatial spectral variations. This work also facilitates detection of transient sources, and we outline an appropriate analysis framework for finding variable sources across the sky. Further customization of the model for transient source analysis reveals its effectiveness in recovering artificial light curves, and enables detection of temporally variable sources across the sky, and among identified sources, we find that approximately 13% exhibit temporal variability, a figure that could be altered by consideration of different time scales and data intervals. We investigated nearly 86,000 small asteroids within the inner solar system by utilizing comprehensive photographic data from the Pan-STARRS1 sky survey. This research focused on identifying potential binary asteroids by searching for photographic evidence of close approaches between an individual asteroid and multiple nearby asteroids of similar size. A statistical model was developed to estimate the likelihood of a binary arrangement for each small asteroid, taking into consideration various physical constraints, orbital patterns within the asteroid belt, and the size distribution of asteroids. This model allowed us to pinpoint the most likely binary configurations, primarily involving small main-belt asteroids with diameters ranging from a few hundred to several thousand meters. A notable binary asteroid candidate emerged in this study, named 354 Pandora, whose orbital pattern suggests a long-periodistic binary arrangement. Furthermore, our research revealed that the majority of potential binary asteroids reside within the inner region of the main asteroid belt, between 2.5 to 3.0 astronomical units from the Sun. This finding is consistent with the presence of binary asteroids containing cohesive, cohesive-free rock mixtures or partially differentiated targets. On the other hand, we found a significantly lower binary asteroid frequency within the outer region of the main asteroid belt, beginning at 3.0 astronomical units from the Sun. This reduction in binary frequencies in the outer region of the main asteroid belt may be attributed to increased breakup distances experienced by asteroids in this region, due to the solar gravitational influence. Our estimates suggest that approximately 7% of the small main-belt asteroids with diameters exceeding 1 kilometer have binary arrangements. Furthermore, our study indicated that the majority of potential binary asteroids exhibit tidal orbits, rather than capture orbits, primarily involving targets with diameters ranging from 10 to 100 kilometers. This research relied on comprehensive photographic data from the Pan-STARRS1 survey, which covered nearly 90% of the inner solar system's asteroid belt, based on precursor surveys from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and the Palomar Sky Survey. This research also yielded a comprehensive catalog of approximate asteroid orbital elements, as well as detailed observations of various asteroid sizes, shapes, and brightness levels. This findings from this research can be applied to ongoing and future sky surveys, which are continually discovering and tracking small asteroids within the inner solar system. This approach enables the Dungeon Master to focus on storytelling and player engagement by delegating world and combat management to the AI. To facilitate this, the Dungeon Master's instructions are kept simple and focused on overall narrative direction, with the AI responsible for refining and executing specific details. This approach has several benefits, including streamlined gameplay, increased player agency, and the ability to handle complex, dynamic environments and storylines. To illustrate this, a sample scenario is provided, along with an analysis of its components and the decision-making processes behind the game elements. The presence of knots in proteins is an intriguing phenomenon that has sparked intense debate, with various explanations suggesting that knots could be a natural consequence of protein formation, providing advantages such as enhanced stability and resistance to degradation. A significant percentage of proteins are found with trefoil knots, and research has shown that the process of knot formation is closely tied to the folding process itself. However, the question of whether and how knots are removed during the protein's life cycle remains poorly understood. By applying magnetic resonance imaging to detect knots and analyze the three-dimensional structure of proteins, our research has revealed unique patterns of knot bending that reflect the environment in which the protein is found, either in its native state or through various biochemical treatments. By comparing these patterns, we were able to identify specific locations where knots are likely to form during the protein's life cycle, and found that certain proteins develop knots in response to different types of stress or chemical treatments, only forming knots when their structure is bent beyond a critical point. On the other hand, some proteins are found with knots that cannot be removed, even with the application of mechanical stress or through the process of unfolding. Interestingly, this subset of proteins with persistent knots exhibits distinct characteristics, including a more complex knot structure and a more open and expansive structure that provides a larger surface area. This is particularly evident with proteins that have a highly curved and trefoil-knotted structure, known as alpha-helical coiled-coils, and these proteins are resistant to change and cannot be converted back to a knotted form. Our research has also revealed unique insights into the process of knot removal, suggesting that it may not be a straightforward process and that proteins with persistent knots have developed mechanisms for adapting to their environment without unwinding their structure. This has significant implications for our understanding of protein dynamics and the role of knots in protein structure and function. On a broader scale, our findings have important applications in fields such as biotechnology and medicine, where the development of stress-induced knots in proteins can present a major obstacle to effective treatment and treatment design. This issue is particularly relevant to proteins that are essential for treating or curing diseases related to gene mutations, where even a single mutation can cause these proteins to become knotted and ineffective. By gaining a deeper understanding of the relationship between protein structure, environment, and function, we can develop more effective and targeted treatments that take into account the unique characteristics of each individual, providing a more personalized approach to medicine and biotechnology. This knowledge can also be used to design new enzymes and proteins with desired properties,

Selberg established the irregular version of the Nambu-Goldstone theorem for relativistic quantum fields, stating that an exact spontaneous symmetry breaking in a generic relativistic quantum field theory at zero temperature results in an irregular number of low-energy bosonic excitations. Since then, this theorem has been applied to a range of situations, including those involving Dirac fermions near a fermion pair condensation, vortices in superfluid/helei3 fluids, and monopoles in 3He superfluid at zero magnetic field. These cases all fall under the category of a irregular Nambu-Goldstone theorem for both relativistic and nonrelativistic systems. In this talk, we will review the basic principles of the irregular Nambu-Goldstone theorem and then discuss some of its key applications in both its original form for relativistic systems and its equivalent form for nonrelativistic systems. In addition to these discussions, we will also examine some of the most notable scenarios, including those mentioned above, as well as some newer research findings. Recent advancements in large language models allow for the generation of sophisticated counterfactuals, which are essential for real-world applications like policy evaluation and reinforcement learning. However, there are limited resources available to train and evaluate these models, particularly in regards to phrasal counterfactual data. In this paper, a novel assessment tool is introduced that leverages freely accessible text to evaluate the ability of language models in generating phrasal counterfactuals. Specifically, it utilizes around 38,000 counterfactual instances derived from around 5,000 articles on Wikipedia. The results show that the average rank of language models based on their ability to generate correct counterfactuals places BART at the top, with around 1000 rankings separating it from the worst model, RoBERTa. Additionally, an in-depth analysis is conducted to understand the factors that influence the performance of these models, revealing that the difficulty varies significantly depending on the type of counterfactual. Moreover, a further analysis is performed to validate the challenging nature of this task, demonstrating that even trained models struggle with around 30% of the counterfactual instances. The evaluation tool, counterfactual data, and analysis are all made publicly available to facilitate further research and development in this critical area. The code has been uploaded to GitHub at https://github.com/ghrase, and the evaluation tool, counterfactual data, and analysis are all available at https://discoproject.github.io/.

In this research, the epitaxial growth of Heusler layers on graphene-sapphire substrates is investigated by means of in-situ X-ray characterization during molecular beam epitaxy. Several factors that influence epitaxial growth were systematically examined, including the temperature, pressure of metal precursors, and the presence of a shadow mask. Equilibrium between four possible epitaxial modes – far-field coalescence, peacock, van der Waals, and central pinhole growth – was found to be maintained by adjusting preparation conditions. A range of conditions that result in coexisting areas of different epitaxial modes was demonstrated, along with the potential for spatial control over epitaxial modes by utilizing a shadow mask. This paves the way for integrating Heusler layers with other materials grown on graphene-sapphire substrates. A comprehensive understanding of Heusler growth on graphene-sapphire substrates is also gained, which could be valuable for transferring graphene-based technologies to silicon wafers. A proposed name for this new layer, HeuGraphene/sapphire (HeuGS), along with its potential for integrating with other materials, is introduced. A comparative study of Heusler growth on bare sapphire substrates and HeuGS is conducted, which reveals that HeuGS results in smoother and more uniform Heusler layers. However, the extent of epitaxial control available with HeuGS is found to be limited due to the presence of graphene flakes. A range of novel Heusler/graphene/sapphire structures with spatial control over epitaxial modes was demonstrated, which could be useful for creating high-speed electronic devices that operate at low temperatures. A potential issue with oxygen incorporation during growth at low temperatures under high vacuum conditions is identified, which could be mitigated by modifying the vacuum chamber to accommodate atmospheric pressure. A range of other Heusler/HeuGS structures grown at low temperatures under high vacuum conditions, which result in excellent crystalline quality and minimal roughness, are presented. A proposal for further research into growing Heusler layers at low temperatures under atmospheric pressure conditions, which could facilitate the transfer of graphene-based technologies to silicon wafers, is made. A range of possible Heusler/HeuGS structures grown at low temperatures under high vacuum conditions, which could facilitate the integration of Heusler layers with other materials grown on graphene-sapphire substrates, are also presented. In traditional multi-label classification, each example is represented by a vector indicating the presence or absence of labels, with no distinction made between independent and dependent labels.  However, many real-world scenarios involve instances that exhibit a single positive label in isolation, without being linked to other related labels, and these instances are often difficult to detect. This paper proposes a novel task, SLIC (Single Label Instance Discovery for Convex Sets), which aims to create a model that, in addition to predicting multi-label outputs, can also identify instances with isolated positive labels. To accomplish this, we introduce a new objective function that learns from the geometric structure of multi-label data. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this model and associated discovery techniques. Moreover, our analysis reveals that there is a direct connection between SLIC and an existing multi-label classification model, making it possible to incorporate additional features that enable the model to discover instances with isolated positive labels. In practical applications, we find that instances with isolated positive labels are frequently absent from datasets, which can lead to biased evaluations if not accounted for. Therefore, it is crucial to demonstrate the generalization of models trained on datasets containing labeled instances with dependent labels. To validate this, we developed a rigorous evaluation protocol that combines both intra-instance and inter-instance diversity, thereby ensuring rigorous assessment of models trained on datasets containing labeled instances with dependent labels. This protocol is applicable to a broad range of multi-label datasets. In contrast to traditional evaluation methods that focus solely on the accuracy of predicted labels, our protocol takes into consideration the geometric structure of multi-label data. To further validate our findings, we created a synthetic dataset with controllable structures, allowing for rigorous analysis of discovery performance in relation to dataset characteristics. In addition, we developed a pioneering approach called Adaptive Single Label Instance Discovery, which enables discovery performance to be evaluated and optimized through the refinement of model parameters. This new net resides in a larger C*-algebra, which is obtained through a specific construction involving the algebra's canonical embedding. When the original C*-algebra was canonical, this process returns to the original net of observables. The original relationship between the algebras is captured in a specific way, defined by the composition of the functors involved. The purpose of this research is to expand the understanding of the GNS construction within the context of statistical mechanics. The new system's algebra is obtained through the tensor product with the original system's algebra. The process of returning to the original system's state is guaranteed, as the 2-categorical adjointation involved ensures that this relationship is preserved. A potential solution involves using machine learning models based on cardiac sound analysis, but these models often fall short due to poor data quality, varying recording techniques, and the complex structure of the body that can distort sound waves.  In an effort to address these challenges, a novel approach is proposed for classifying cardiac sounds that incorporates two key features: the first deals with noise reduction by removing additive interference from the recordings, and the second addresses shape transformations that affect the signal, such as lung sounds that can cause deformation and time-shifts, common in real-world recordings. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Unfortunately, training accurate machine learning models on private health data is challenging due to privacy concerns. In this paper, we tackle the issue of constructing a robust activity recognition model using federated transfer learning on wearable health data. Specifically, we develop a framework that leverages data from two entities: a healthcare provider and a data generator. The healthcare provider possesses activity data without labels, while the data generator provides labeled data from a different domain. We demonstrate that exchanging only a subset of the healthcare provider's data allows for effective training of the base model by the data generator and subsequent transfer learning by the healthcare provider. Our proposed method, FedHealth, facilitates seamless healthcare services while ensuring the privacy and security of individual data. Our experimental evaluations on real wearable health data in both scenario one (where the data distributions are similar) and scenario two (where the data distributions differ significantly) showcase the robustness and versatility of FedHealth. Our results indicate that FedHealth outperforms conventional machine learning models by approximately 8% when the data distributions are similar and achieves nearly 5% better performance than conventional machine learning models when the data distributions differ significantly. Our proposed framework for FedHealth is scalable, secure, and private and can be applied across various activity recognition contexts including fitness sports, elderly care, and military training. Our code is available at https://github.com/ChangXun yuan/FedHealth. Even so, we find certain combinations of leptoquark groups, specifically those with charges (1/3, 0), (0, -1), (1/3, -1), and (2/3, -1), can exceed single leptoquark production rates at higher energy levels, particularly with 13-100 TeV proton-proton collisions. For these scenarios, we establish event creation criteria and investigate how often these leptoquark pairs would be mistakenly identified as single leptoquark events, with estimates ranging from 10% to 90% misclassification, heavily influenced by energy levels and specific leptoquark masses. To this end, we outline strategies for the Large Hadron Collider experiments to search for these leptoquark pairs among single leptoquark event candidates, starting with the assumption that single leptoquark production rates have been adequately accounted for. If successful, such a detection would mark the first instance of pair production at the Large Hadron Collider and provide precise information on certain leptoquark groups, including those with charges (1/3, -1) and (2/3, -1). We analyzed a comprehensive database of 112 galaxies with measured molecular gas reservoirs, 21cm neutral hydrogen spectra, and a comprehensive line library including far-infrared molecular lines, both optically thick and thin, culminating in a study of external stimulation of molecular gas through the subthermal radiation of CO and CI. Our findings indicate that the bulk of molecular gas is adequately explained by a single, uniform model, with a notable deviation in low-mass galaxies containing massive starbursts. Furthermore, we discovered that the excess stimulation of CO and CI lines, beyond the level expected by molecular mass alone, are typically minimal, with an estimated 10% of galaxies displaying some level of such stimulation. Our study suggests possible indicators for galaxies experiencing significant stimulation of their molecular gas, including galaxies with unusually strong emission from CI or CO, low CO to HI ratios in comparison to mass, low dust temperatures in comparison to mass, extensive star formation in low-mass galaxies, or galaxies with both active and dormant black holes. In such cases, we estimate that the radiation could result in additional stimulation of an additional 10-100 bar of gas, available for future starbursts or a supermassive black hole growth. Consequently, this study implies that external stimulation of molecular gas may have a more modest impact than previously anticipated, yet it still has the potential to drive additional star formation or black hole growth in a minority of galaxies. Our findings highlight the significance of observing both thin and thick lines, as well as the potential value of future observations targeting both CO and CI lines, as well as far-infrared spectral lines, in a broader line library, for a comprehensive understanding of the relationships between different components of galaxies. Our study also results in a new, improved formula estimating the stimulation of molecular gas, expressed in units of thermal energy, as a function of both density and optical depth, combining both CO and CI lines, as well as far-infrared dust temperatures, with implications for both observational and simulation studies. Lastly, we provide individual line spectra for all 112 analyzed galaxies, as well as various reference spectra for simulation purposes.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole mergers occurring at large distances. To efficiently find these signals, a new method quickly identifies potential matches between PTA data and merged binary waveforms, focusing on patterns in the data rather than the waveforms themselves. This approach generates synthetic signals that resemble detected patterns, allowing for a faster comparison to actual data. Our analysis shows that this method can effectively detect signals with moderate to high precision, meeting the standards of current PTA data, while also outperforming alternative approaches in terms of computational expense. Furthermore, by analyzing the effects of precision on computing time, we found that increasing the precision beyond a certain point does not significantly improve the results, and found ways to optimize the process for a real-world dataset used in PTA research. This optimization demonstrates that it's possible to search for one week's worth of data on a few GPUs within a few months, indicating that searching through larger datasets of PTA data will become feasible in the near future. This progress is crucial for discovering individual merger signals and understanding the characteristics of massive binary mergers, and it paves the way for exploring other predicted phenomena, such as massive black hole binaries with misaligned spins, and barred black hole mergers, which also leave distinctive signals that PTA experiments can detect. This project was implemented using the GWebin framework, an open-source platform for analyzing PTA data and predicting the characteristics of gravitational wave signals. This framework, and the efficiency-search algorithm developed in this research, are available for public use. This research was conducted using computing resources provided by the University of California, Berkeley, and the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center. This paper is the third in a series of three research papers related to detecting individual supermassive black hole mergers with PTA experiments, which also include the papers titled: Predicted signals from individual supermassive black hole mergers in Pulsar Timing Array data (2020) and Detecting individual supermassive black hole mergers with Pulsar Timing Array experiments (2019). Unlike traditional ASEP models, this graded velocity model does not automatically converge to TASEP behavior, even when time approaches infinity. This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address key epidemiological questions. A distinction is drawn between early epidemic models and subsequent period models. Early models, primarily logistic-based and SEIR-type models, effectively captured the pandemic's initial course but struggled to anticipate the emergence of severe symptoms and high-mortality rate groups. These models led to important policy recommendations but ultimately fell short in providing insights into critical issues facing public health officials during the pandemic's latter stages. In contrast, period models explored other important transmission dynamics, such as asymptomatic transmission, severe symptom onset rates, and high-mortality rate groups, which were observed during this stage. These models offered a more nuanced understanding of the epidemic's development and guided crucial decisions regarding vaccination rollout and targeting strategies. We highlight the value of both early and period models in contributing to a deeper understanding of the pandemic and emphasize the diversity of mathematical frameworks used to model outbreaks. These models can be broadly categorized across four key viewpoints: ordinary differential equations, delay equations, fractional differential equations, and individual-based models. Each viewpoint offers distinct methodological advantages that align with specific research questions and data characteristics. We also examine the various approaches used to estimate key model parameters and evaluate models based on available data. These methods include machine learning, optimization techniques, and multiple scaling approaches to match models with data at different spatial and temporal levels. We conclude by discussing the challenges facing model developers and public health officials and explore the many unanswered questions that arose during the pandemic, such as developing models that account for different vaccination distribution policies, the impact of various transmission rates, and the best methods for scaling and transferring models to new settings. We hope that future researchers will address these challenges and provide a framework for modeling outbreaks that can guide policy decisions and inform our understanding of epidemic dynamics during similar public health crises. In the process, they can draw on the numerous research avenues opened up by the pandemic, including but not limited to, individual-based modeling, machine learning, and the many unresolved theoretical issues in differential equations that arose from the analysis of pandemic data. In the appendix, we provide a list of models reviewed in this study along with their key characteristics and research questions they aimed to address. We also include a brief overview of the various machine learning approaches used to forecast the pandemic and outline the general methodology used in these studies. Furthermore, we examine the different spatial and temporal scaling approaches used to match models with data and present a list of individual-based models used to forecast the pandemic, along with the research questions they aimed to address and the data
