To improve the efficiency of Navier-Stokes solutions on the macroscopic scale, a new rapid solver is proposed that leverages a hybrid physics-mathematics approach. This approach combines the nonlinear solving of a compact shallow water model with a system of algebraic equations, utilizing a novel framework called network of algebraic operators. To enhance convergence and accelerate solutions, the solver incorporates a deep learning-based neural network. This network, trained on a vast dataset of turbulent flows, provides an initial, approximate solution to the system of algebraic equations. To validate the solver and demonstrate its effectiveness, it was applied to three well-documented cases involving turbulent flows with complex geometries. These results show that the solver achieves rapid and accurate solutions, with an order of magnitude improvement in computation time while maintaining a high level of precision. This is particularly evident in scenarios where high-resolution models would require an impractically long time to solve, such as in flows through constrictions and over weirs. This research highlights the potential of this solver to efficiently model a broad range of fluid dynamics scenarios. High-dynamic-range (HDR) imaging is a technique that combines multiple photos captured at different exposure levels to produce a single image with a wider intensity range, mimicking the human visual system.  This research presents an innovative method for HDR imaging using only a smartphone, without any additional hardware.  The proposed technique captures two images at optimized exposure levels or uses images pre-stored on the smartphone, and then employs a mobile HDR implementation based on focal point selection.  The resulting image outperforms the smartphone's auto-exposure control and standard HDR methods, and is comparable to a desktop HDR reference implementation.  The proposed technique also includes an adaptive fusion method that accounts for tonal differences between captured images, further enhancing the mobile HDR experience.  The findings of this research were verified through extensive testing and comparison with a desktop reference implementation, and the proposed technique was found to be suitable for various smartphone models.  The proposed mobile HDR solution has been made available to the public through open-source code. In this work, we explore a new concept we call causal neural learning, which integrates causal learning and neural networks. A well-performing model on a causal learning task is not necessarily a well-performing model on a supervised learning task with the same data, and this distinction's significance is compounded by the varied forms that supervised learning can take. We demonstrate how the underlying structure of a dataset, expressed as a causal graph, influences both supervised and unsupervised learning using simple examples. We also examine how different loss functions affect learning from a noisy, sythetic dataset generated based on a specified causal graph. Furthermore, we investigate how different learning methods derive benefits from a dataset generated under a particular causal scenario. We propose a novel assessment metric that measures a model's ability to accurately predict labels based on features derived from a causal learning framework. This metric enables a comparison of supervised learning outcomes resulting from diverse causal learning scenarios. We also explore the relationship between these outcomes and standard supervised learning benchmarks. We propose an intuitive, graphical representation of the conditions under which a particular Markov network accurately predicts labels based on the features obtained from a causal learning framework. This representation allows us to visually identify the conditions necessary for valid generalization of a model to a new dataset. We demonstrate how to translate this graphical representation into a numerical form that corresponds to the proposed assessment metric. We leverage this representation and metric to examine the performance of different learning methods on a dataset generated under a particular causal scenario. We find that only a small subset of these methods yields satisfactory results. We also examine the performance of a neural network on a dataset obtained through intervention, and compare it to the performance on a dataset obtained through observation. We observe a significant discrepancy between these performance metrics. We propose an alternative approach to learning from a dataset obtained through observation, which involves an additional intervention step and yields a better performance metric. This note presents a new version of the b-principle with an added caveat, referring to a particular conjecture known as the Mumford Conjecture. A more expansive version of the b-principle, which the authors term the strong b-principle, holds true if and only if the Mumford Conjecture is valid. The strong b-principle can be viewed as a higher congruence relation that mirrors the structure of the weak b-principle, which in turn resembles a congruence relation. The weak b-principle can be stated as follows: for mapping categories F and G, there exists a bijection between congruences that are natural and invariant with respect to F, and mappings from the base category of F to the orbit space of G. This bijection is categorized, meaning it respects the structure of mapping categories. The weak b-principle has been established for a wide range of mapping categories, but the strong b-principle remains unconfirmed and is equivalent to the unresolved Mumford Conjecture. The authors of this note demonstrate that if the strong b-principle is assumed to hold, it implies a significant generalization of the Mumford Conjecture. Furthermore, the authors propose a more expansive form of the strong b-principle that they believe is equivalent to the complete Mumford Conjecture. The authors also clarify that the strong b-principle can be applied to map categories with properties of differentiability, specifically showing it is applicable to categories such as diffeomorphisms, embeddings, and smooth embeddings. The authors conclude this note by highlighting the relationship between the strong b-principle and the abstract embedding theorem, which forms the foundational aspect of the Mumford Conjecture. The note ends by posing the question of whether the strong b-principle can be confirmed through the use of the full Mumford Conjecture, or if there are any other conditions under which the principle would be valid. The authors propose a possible strategy for proving the principle in a more general context. The note also includes an appendix that details the relationship between the strong b-principle and the full Mumford Conjecture, as well as the derivation of the expanded form of the principle from the assumptions of the context in which it is applicable. The note ends by providing a historical context for the development of the b-principle and the conjectures related to it. The authors of this note include Professors Mrowka, S.S. and Tao, T. For our paper titled at {\em L2Explorer}: A Eternal Reinforcement Learning Evaluation Ecosystem,
Reinforcement learning effectiveness is commonly assessed through multiple metrics,
including cumulative rewards, episode lengths, and a combination of both.
However, a static evaluation criterion rewards a agent as much for exploiting
existing knowledge as it does for discovering new information.
To address this issue, we present L2Explorer, a cutting-edge evaluation framework
based on a combined exploration-exploitation strategy that valuates a agent
on two distinct dimensions: the duration it continues to innovate in a limitless
environment and the optimal solutions it discovers.
Unlike a endless timeline, L2Explorer uses a fixed timeframe for both testing
and validation, resulting in a compact evaluation framework with three key components:
(1) Generative Level and Challenge Design: a tool for creating and managing endless
generative environments, (2) Evaluation Criteria: a method for calculating a combined
score based on a combination of rewards and discovery depth, and (3) Comparative Analysis: a
feature that enables side-by-side comparison of multiple agents.
We put L2Explorer through a series of tests and evaluations to assure its practicality,
precision, and effectiveness.
In particular, we found a fixed timeframe to be particularly effective in distinguishing
between high-performance agent variants.
To demonstrate the versatility of L2Explorer, we also developed two distinct agent variants: simple and complex.
When evaluated on a straightforward task, the complex agent outperformed the simple agent.
However, when evaluated on a more challenging task, the simple agent proved more capable.
Our research on L2Explorer highlights a significant issue with ongoing reinforcement learning evaluation methods.
It also presents a novel, eternal evaluation ecosystem that addresses this issue.
Our results show that L2Explorer-based evaluation methods validate the challenging nature of tasks accurately.
As such, they provide valuable feedback to researchers and developers.
Our research on L2Explorer was conducted in the context of text-based adventure games.
However, the framework and methodology we presented are applicable to a broad range of evaluation tasks that involve ongoing exploration and validation.

Monitoring declarative processes involves tracking the satisfaction of conditions in processes that follow rules and conditions, without direct access to the underlying activities. Despite the benefits of a surveillance-based approach, previous methods require initial access to process data, limiting their use in situations where processes are partially known. Existing exploration techniques, on the other hand, assume that process data is fully accessible, also barring partial knowledge scenarios. In response to these limitations, we introduce a method that enables both surveillance and exploration of processes with partially known data, utilizing feedback from the environment in response to newly encountered activities. The proposed approach generates a set of rules that, when combined with initial process data, guarantee process validity for both declarative processes and dynamic systems. We prove the correctness of these rules through a formal analysis, and demonstrate the practical application of our method to two examples. The resulting process is then compared to equivalent static processes, revealing a significant reduction in process complexity. The proposed method surpasses existing methods in situations where processes are partially known, offering greater flexibility with minimal increase in process complexity. The underlying approach also allows for easy adaptation to different environments, facilitating seamless use in various situations. We outline an analytic approach to compactifying spaces, demonstrating that it results in an algebraic compactification when the underlying field is a finite extension of the rational numbers. We also examine specific instances of parameterized spaces that, when considered in their most basic form, contain singularities that cannot be removed using the methods available to us, and therefore require more advanced techniques to establish irreducibility and completeness. Our study of these spaces aims to expand the range of applications for the results of McKean and the first author, who previously established the completeness of an algebraic family of compact Riemann surfaces within a specific parameter space, and demonstrated that this space is Archimedean in nature. We subsequently discovered an alternative, more straightforward proof of their completeness theorem. Our research also yields the irreducibility of a particular space defined by a set of polynomial equations, and demonstrates that this space is both complete and compact when limited to finite extensions of the rational numbers. We believe that our analysis of this space may be utilized as a model for examining other, similar spaces. We used HST/ACS and VLT/MUSE observations to examine the morphology, motion, and chemical composition of galaxies in a cluster that existed approximately 3.7 billion years ago, during a rapid period of galaxy construction. This analysis uncovered galaxies with irregular star-forming disks and central bulge formations, likely the result of minor mergers with small gas-rich galaxies. This theory is supported by simulations of galaxy interactions, motion data indicating these galaxies had high relative speeds, and chemical analysis showing they had high levels of gas. These galaxies, with masses similar to that of the Milky Way, demonstrated distinct star-formation and gas properties. Despite their disrupted appearances, these galaxies showed no ongoing supernova or supermassive black hole activity. This led to the conclusion that their bulges formed through the collisionless gravitational effects of past minor mergers rather than active galactic mergers. This finding is unusual because it contrasts with the common perception that galaxy bulges are primarily formed through massive mergers. This cluster from the early universe provides valuable insights into the role of minor mergers in galaxy bulge formation, and supports models suggesting its low occurrence in the present day is because massive galaxies in the present day have largely merged with each other. Furthermore, this research highlights the short lifetimes of some galaxies, with some displaying distorted shapes for only 500 million years. This cluster from the early universe, with its diverse range of galaxy ages, also offers valuable information about the rates of galaxy construction and destruction. This is particularly evident for disk galaxies with minimal star formation, which can transform into bulge galaxies in as little as 500 million years. This research provides a window into the short-lived nature of many galaxies from the early universe, with many being destroyed or transformed within 1-2 billion years. This is consistent with the common perception that the universe has been continuously building and reconstructing itself since its inception. This research was published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society Volume 495, Issue 1, January 2020, pp. 114-133.

On November 7, 2004, a particularly intense solar flare occurred, accompanied by significant radiation levels observed in France, Austria, Germany, Greece, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland, and Ukraine. Decades of data from neutron monitors around the world were analyzed to study this event, and our findings reveal that the radiation surge was composed of two components with distinct temporal patterns. The first part of the radiation increase aligned with cosmic-ray watch clocks, suggesting it was influenced by Earth's magnetic field variation, while the second component followed a power law time course typical of solar proton energy spectra. This unusual combination of time patterns and energy spectra is previously unreported in solar proton data, and our observations also reveal that the radiation levels at higher latitudes took longer to decrease than those at lower latitudes. This unusual event provides new insights into the behavior of solar protons and their relationship with Earth's magnetic field, and our findings are consistent with recent simulations of solar proton interactions with Earth's magnetic field. Our analysis indicates that the radiation levels observed in Europe during this event were equivalent to those of a 10 GeV cosmic-ray particle beam. Our study used the most comprehensive dataset available, representing the longest duration radiation surge detected on Earth since neutron monitors began collecting data in 1955. Our findings have significant implications for understanding the complex interactions between solar protons, Earth's magnetic field, and the effects they have on radiation levels and cosmic-ray streams around the planet. Our analysis of this unprecedented event also offers valuable insights for the safety of people in flight due to increased cosmic radiation levels caused by solar proton events. The observation of a rapidly spinning (104.7 km/s) giant gas planet around a bright subgiant star highlights an intriguing phenomenon where the angular momentum of the planet exceeds expectations based on standard core formation and migration models. By analyzing light curves and spectral data, our research reveals that the planet's likely axis of rotation aligns with the star's rotational axis, and we find evidence for absorption features that could be attributed to the planet's atmosphere. However, the absence of a significant orbital eccentricity means the planet's angular momentum cannot be explained by tidal interactions. We propose a few possible scenarios, including the possibility that the planet's spin was influenced by a massive companion that is no longer present, or that the spin was generated internally through convection and differential rotation within the planet and the star. We also observe a potential asymmetry in the light curves that could be related to the effects of the planet's spin, and we suggest future observations could confirm the presence of the proposed axis-dependent absorption features, which would have significant implications for our understanding of planetary formation and the evolution of gas giants within the habitable zones of stars. The unique characteristics of this system also make it an appropriate subject for further study, including the use of direct imaging and spectroscopy, and mass-loss and exoplanetary angular momentum transfer models. Ultimately, our research underscores the importance of incorporating the effects of spin and magnetic field on the formation and evolution of planets and stars, as well as the value of multi-disciplinary observations and simulations in fully understanding this complex system. The rapid dissemination of fake news on social media platforms is not only harmful to individual users but also poses a significant threat to society as a whole. Although deep-learning-based fake-news-detection techniques have made significant progress in recent years, maintaining their effectiveness over time is a major concern. This issue is addressed in this paper, which presents a novel approach that employs meta-learning to effectively detect emerging counterfeit news in social media environments. This approach leverages information from previous counterfeit-news-detection tasks to enhance the efficacy of its neural network model, which is then refined to maximize similarity with local data. The resulting model achieves high accuracy in counterfeit-news detection on Facebook without prior knowledge of the data. This finding is supported by experimental results obtained using real-world social media data. Furthermore, our approach demonstrates superior performance in comparison to conventional transfer learning techniques. Additionally, our method exhibits robust performance when confronted with new, previously unseen counterfeit news types. This is demonstrated through additional experiments conducted using real-world datasets. The code for this research has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghr96/MCNDN. Moreover, an optimized version of our model, termed MCNDN-512, has been submitted to the CCF-CRC-CONVENE Big Data Challenge 2022 hosted by the China Academy of Sciences. According to the official evaluation results, MCNDN-512 ranked first among the 12 teams that participated in the challenge, as confirmed through personal communication with the challenge organizers. This model has also been successfully applied to counterfeit-news-detection tasks on WeChat, another popular social media platform. The results obtained with WeChat data are presented in the additional files available with the online version of this paper. The challenges and opportunities associated with evaluating the performance of fake-news-detection systems are also discussed in this paper. Although the approach presented in this paper is applicable to other classification tasks that involve future data, the primary focus of this research is on counterfeit-news detection in social media environments. The approach introduced in this paper offers valuable insights that can be applied to other such environments. Furthermore, the challenge of evaluating the performance of these systems is a major obstacle that must be addressed through the development of innovative methods that consider the dynamic nature of real-world data. This research paper examines a recurrent transport equation with the presence of a force term, initially formulated by V. Da Prato and J. Lions in 1972, and later extended to equations with time-dependent domains by H. Amann in 1989. We aim to investigate the recurrence and transport equations where the domain and forcing terms vary with time, and demonstrate the existence and uniqueness of the solution for these equations, even in the presence of discontinuities, provided that the domain changes at a rate that allows it to remain connected and recurrent. Furthermore, we establish that the solution remains recurrent under the same conditions. Additionally, we provide specific examples of time-dependent domains that satisfy these conditions, including those with moving boundaries and surfaces, and demonstrate that the recurrence of the solution is influenced by the presence of singular points where the domain changes suddenly, leading to the solution becoming non-recurrent in these instances. Lastly, we offer an alternative approach to proving the recurrence of the solution that does not rely on the estimation of the $L^1$ norm. This research was motivated by the need to extend the results from our previous paper to the case of a transport equation with discontinuous diffusion coefficients, and to investigate the role of singular points in changing the recurrence of the solution. A new concept of golay complementary structures is introduced, where the golay pairs from different time phases and frequency phases form a complete complementary set. This novel idea extends the traditional golay complementary sequences to 2D signals, enabling multiple signal coexistence without cross-terms and interference. To facilitate seamless integration, golay complementary structures in time and frequency domains are designed, including arrays of golay complementary sequences, matrix-based golay complementary designs, and cyclic golay complementary structures. These designs can be implemented in various applications, including wireless communication systems, radar technology, and spectroscopic analysis. The proposed method provides a versatile tool for creating golay complementary structures with diverse signal characteristics, meeting the requirements of different coexistence scenarios. The paper presents a range of designs, from fundamental golay complementary sequences to complex cyclic structures, and offers a design framework for implementing these structures in various scenarios. The proposed golay complementary structures can be applied to various contexts, including simultaneous signal detection in radar and spectroscopy, multi-carrier wireless communication systems, and spread-spectrum communication technologies. The paper concludes by outlining a roadmap for further advancements in 2D golay complementary structures, including designs for larger set sizes and structures with increased periodicity. All-electronic valley interference has been directly observed with an atomic resolution, utilizing low-energy helium ion scanning to create nanostructure arrays on silicon surfaces.  These interactions result in unique patterns of spin accumulation along dimer rows, varying depending on whether they are composed of dimer units with either the same or different atomic arrangements.  This phenomenon is caused by the difference in valley interference patterns brought about by the slight difference in bond lengths within these structures.  Researchers have also discovered that valley interference is influenced by the curvature of dimer rows, presenting either positive or negative impact on spin accumulation distribution.  This discovery's implications are explored in potential applications of silicon-based quantum computing.  Valley interference patterns can be manipulated through helium ion scanning, enabling controlled valley interaction and spin transfer.  This finding complements previous discoveries related to valley interference and spin accumulation in silicon, offering a more advanced level of control over quantum states.  All observations were verified using a range of techniques including scanning tunneling microscopy, low-temperature scanning tunneling spectroscopy, and ab initio calculations.  This research was published in the journal Nature Communications. The study involved an interdisciplinary team of scientists from the Paul Scherrer Institute, ETH Zurich, and the University of Bern.  The lead authors of the study are Dr. Christian Tung, Dr. Yves Martin, Dr. Fabian W. Dahl, Dr. Christian R. Ast, and Prof. Dr. Klaus Kern.  The research was supported by the Swiss National Science Foundation, the ETH Zurich, and the University of Bern.  The findings have significant implications for silicon-based quantum technologies and provide a means of controlling valley interference and spin transfer at the atomic and molecular level.  The discovery of spin and valley interference patterns in silicon dimers also paves the way for further advancements in quantum state control and silicon-based quantum computing. Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively learn from just a single observed time series representation of the system. This limitation hinders our ability to fully explore the internal mechanics and design of these complex systems. To address this challenge, our research introduces an end-to-end learning framework based on graph neural networks that automatically discovers the system's dynamics and optimal architecture, using only a single time series representation as input. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach on real-world datasets, including both synthetic and empirical data, and show that it not only outperforms a range of benchmark models but also yields a compact and interpretable representation of the system's internal structure and dynamics. Our findings validate the capabilities of our framework in uncovering the underlying architecture and dynamics of complex systems and pave the way for its broader applications in fields like system identification and design. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghulam-sabih/learning-dynamics-and-architecture-of-complex-systems.

We establish a formula counting the number of distinct partitions of a specific type that arise in the course of constructing a particular construct, known as the universal construction through the interaction of functors and functions between categories, utilizing the fundamental properties of the Grothendieck group and Weyl group. This formula is subsequently applied to obtain results on the structure of specific constructs, such as the universal construction involving the Tate functor, thereby yielding an invariant known as the Tate cohomology, and providing a proof of the classification of the universal constructs involving the group functor, namely the extension groups. This in turn leads to an interpretation of the results in terms of an established concept, known as group completion. Furthermore, an analogy with an analogous result in the field of algebraic topology is established, where the universal construct involving the reduced suspension functor is shown to be equivalent to the Eilenberg-MacLane spectrum S, thereby yielding an intrinsic definition of S in terms of the abstract constructs and categories. This research was conducted in collaboration with the mathematics community through posting the results on a website dedicated to preprints. Since then, one of the readers suggested an alternative approach to the results related to the universal constructs involving the group functor, providing an equivalent but more straightforward proof. This preprint is part of a broader website project dedicated to exploring and analyzing the connections between the constructs and categories, with a focus on deriving results and proving or disproving conjectures, and is continuously updated with the input and feedback from the mathematics community. A significant challenge in treating stroke lies in identifying appropriate therapies given a specific type of large ischemic brain lesion called MCA territory. To achieve this, it's essential to accurately predict the extent of cerebral damage caused by a blockage in the middle cerebral artery. To predict this damage, researchers rely on models that combine imaging data with a biological response. However, existing models struggle to account for the uncertainty in both the data and the biological response. To address this limitation, a new generative model is proposed that simultaneously handles data and biological uncertainty while predicting cerebral damage caused by an MCA blockage. The new model combines a variational autoencoder with the ability to draw samples from the data distribution, a discriminator similar to one used in the GAN framework, and a stochastic biological response model. By leveraging these components, the model minimizes the difference between the reconstructed data and the actual data, the uncertainty associated with the predicted biological response, and the certainty associated with the actual biological response. The proposed model outperforms existing methods in evaluating the size of the cerebral lesion caused by an MCA blockage based on MRI images acquired before the stroke. Additionally, the model accurately estimates the treatment effectiveness of a particular therapy called moAb against an MCA blockage. The code for this model is available at https://github.com/aliutendian/StrokeSeg.git, and the data used in this study is available at http://www.cbrain.ca. The proposed model has been tested using a publicly available dataset called the CMA dataset which consists of 50 MRI images acquired before the stroke and corresponding cerebral lesion caused by an MCA blockage with 25 images used for training and 25 images used for validation. The model has also been tested using a private dataset called the Montreal dataset which consists of 50 MRI images acquired before the stroke and corresponding cerebral lesion caused by an MCA blockage with 25 images used for training and 25 images used for validation. The proposed model has been compared with existing methods in evaluating the size of the cerebral lesion caused by an MCA blockage based on MRI images acquired before the stroke using the Montreal dataset which consists of 50 MRI images acquired before the stroke and corresponding cerebral lesion caused by an MCA blockage with 25 images used for training and 25 images used for validation. The proposed model has also been compared with existing methods in evaluating the size of the cerebral lesion caused by an MCA blockage based on MRI images acquired before the stroke using the accuracy and the mean absolute error as metrics

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, efficiently developing GP 2 programs poses difficulties, primarily stemming from the time-consuming nature of graph matching. To overcome this limitation, the GP 2 framework incorporates a type of rooted rule that can be matched rapidly, given certain conditions are met. In order to accelerate the development process for verifiable programs, the GP 2 compiler has been enhanced to cater for rooted rules, featuring a user-friendly syntax similar to regular GP 2 rules. Furthermore, the compiler now generates optimized rooted rules that, in addition to conditions, are associated with a set of required graph nodes, effectively guiding the application of these rules during program analysis. As proof of its utility, the GP 2 compiler has been successfully applied to a previously inaccessible program verification problem. In this case, a program was made verifiable following a GP 2-based validation procedure, despite the presence of loop constructs that initially appeared to present a challenge. In a more comprehensive example, the compiler has also been utilized to enable the validation of a program featuring recursive function calls, subject to certain conditions. In both instances, the GP 2 compiler's efficiency and flexibility were found to outperform a manually optimized version, demonstrating the benefits of using the compiler in program development processes. In addition to its application in program verification, the GP 2 compiler has also been employed in a program transformation task, involving the insertion of specific nodes within an existing program, provided that certain conditions are met. In this scenario, the compiler was found to provide a more concise and efficient solution compared to a manually optimized alternative. In conclusion, the GP 2 compiler has been designed to ease the development of verifiable programs, offering a range of benefits including increased productivity, reduced development time, and increased program validity, as demonstrated in the accompanying case studies. In its current form, the compiler is suitable for a broad range of applications, including program validation, data transformation, and program transformation, following the GP 2 methodology. In order to facilitate further development and verification tasks, the GP 2 compiler source code has been made available online, awaiting the contribution of interested researchers and developers. In this paper, the GP 2 compiler has been presented as a tool for developing verifiable programs, with an emphasis on demonstrating its ease of use, following a step-by-step introduction to its basic concepts and features. In recent years, attribute extraction has seen significant progress, with many approaches being categorized into two main types: single-instance and multi-instance methods. Single-instance methods, relying on classification models, have achieved high accuracy but struggle with unfamiliar attributes. In contrast, multi-instance methods, utilizing clustering algorithms, demonstrate robustness towards novel attributes but subpar performance. To bridge this gap, a hybrid framework is proposed, integrating the strengths of both single-instance and multi-instance methods by employing a contrastive learning-based attribute representation structure. This structure consists of a classification module for familiar attributes and a clustering module for novel ones, with a contrastive learning block to ensure a unified attribute representation. The proposed framework has been extensively tested on six datasets, yielding superior results compared to state-of-the-art attribute extraction methods. Moreover, it demonstrates versatility by successfully adapting to novel attributes without the need for additional data. The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/zhengyangt/Unified-Structure-for-Attribute-Extraction. The proposed unified structure provides a valuable insight into designing robust attribute extraction systems that can efficiently handle both familiar and novel attributes. A graph theory context, specifically within the framework of symmetric networks, provides the setting for an interesting problem that has been previously solved for a finite number of congruence relations. However, an extension to an infinite number of congruence relations derived from a particular infinite set of 2-group generators reveals an initially unexpected result. Specifically, it was found that an infinite number of star normal quotient networks can be constructed using a specific type of twisted wreath structure. These constructed networks possess unique properties, such as being highly symmetric and incapable of being minimized, and they outperform the existing classical cage structures in regards to maximum vertex distance. These findings also enable the creation of large-scale complex structures with a specific design criterion in mind and provide an infinite number of options for selecting a suitable one. These results were obtained by developing novel approaches to generate and analyze the proposed structures and by establishing connections between them and established results in number theory, specifically involving the properties of certain sequences associated with Lucas numbers. These sequences, in turn, were found to be related to the function $f(x) = x^2 - 68x -1$, which has a significance connection to the generated structures. These structures can be further classified into distinct subcategories based on the properties of their generated sequences, and they have an isomorphism relationship with certain network configurations derived from a specific set of 2-group generators. These results also imply the existence of an infinite number of graphs with specific design criteria, such as being highly symmetric, incapable of being minimized, and containing the maximum possible vertex distance, and they provide a novel general formula for these types of graphs. These structures can be further extended to include the harmonic twisted wreath networks, which are defined as the network obtained by replacing the central ring of a harmonic twisted wreath structure with an odd cycle. These harmonic twisted wreath networks have an additional property of being edge-transitive. Working with categorical data for model selection and feature reduction is a common challenge in many high-dimensional scenarios. Categorical variables often take on a large number of levels, leading to extensive sparsity patterns and difficulties in achieving stable estimates using traditional methods. To address this issue, Group Lasso has been a popular and effective tool; however, its application is complicated by the need to treat each level of a categorical variable as a separate feature. To simplify the process while utilizing Group Lasso, a new penalized method is proposed by treating each group of continuous features or categorical variables as a unit. This results in the development of an iterative algorithm tailored for polyedral fuctions, allowing for a range of regularization options, including Group Lasso, Elastic Net, and Group Elastic Net. The new method, called Strong Group Iterative Shrinkage and Selection (SGISS), leverages an iterative shrinkage strategy, effortlessly handling complex sparsity patterns and overcoming the challenge of determining the number of groups required for suitable model selection. The development of efficient convex relaxation techniques and the application of a dual representation enable the derivation of a computationally feasible and exact reconstruction algorithm from the projection of the current estimate onto the constraint set. This results in an adaptive and efficient iterative scheme that seamlessly handles difficult scenarios with a large number of levels in categorical data, even with the Group Lasso criterion. The methodology is further extended to develop a new procedure, called Strong Group in Extreme (SGE), for addressing situations with an extremely large number of levels, where the number of levels in a categorical variable is comparable to the sample size. Theoretical support for the asymptotic consistency of SGIS is provided, alongside an exhaustive numerical study that includes a real-world dataset. The proposed methodology is applicable to a broad range of regularization techniques, offering a versatile and powerful tool with numerous potential applications in various machine learning tasks. The corresponding R code for SGIS and SGE is available online. The paper considers the case where the number of levels in a categorical variable is fixed, assuming n,k,Q→∞ with n→∞. Theoretical support for the asymptotic consistency of SGIS is provided for the case where the number of levels in a categorical variable is fixed, assuming n,k,Q→∞ with n→∞. The case where the number of levels in a categorical variable is fixed is used to investigate the relationship between the proposed method and Group Lasso, demonstrating that the two methods are equivalent under the condition that the number of levels in a categorical variable is fixed. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous tasks, yet the scope of these models remains unclear due to their ability to generate informative explanations. Current assessment methods primarily focus on the model's ability to provide relevant answers without evaluating the quality of the underlying reasoning. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel methodology centered on large language models' ability to incorporate structured knowledge. We develop a framework, called Insight Infusion, which evaluates the model's capacity to integrate knowledge from multiple sources, combining them into a structured form that reflects the underlying relationships and patterns. We apply this framework to evaluate a range of large language models on a range of tasks, incorporating both human-created datasets and freely available web information. Our findings reveal that models performance varies significantly, depending on the level of task complexity and available knowledge. Ultimately, our research provides a foundation for a broader understanding of large language models that prioritizes the analysis of their underlying reasoning mechanisms. Our work is available at https://github.com/ghrua/skill.

High-resolution vector maps are widely used in various applications such as GPS navigation, online mapping services and automated driving. To achieve real-time rendering, these maps often employ a technique called line connection anti-aliasing to counteract the ringing effect caused by the abrupt line termination, thereby ensuring a smooth and visually appealing display. However, the computational cost of this technique is significant, primarily due to the numerous operations involved in determining intersection points between lines and the rendering of curved segments to depict anti-aliased line connections. To address this challenge, we present an optimized solution for line connection anti-aliasing on vector maps by introducing a simplified algorithm that reduces the computational burden while maintaining visual consistency with the original technique. We also explore a range of sub-optimization strategies to further minimize rendering time, making our solution suitable for real-time applications involving high-resolution vector maps. In a comparative analysis with the original technique, our optimized line connection anti-aliasing method achieves a notable 12.78% reduction in processing time on a single GPU core. To illustrate the practical effectiveness of our solution, we incorporated the optimized technique into a demo application that demonstrates line connection anti-aliasing on a massive vector map, resulting in a 14.73% decrease in rendering time on a mid-range GPU. Our research indicates that line connection anti-aliasing can be efficiently integrated into real-time applications involving vector maps with minimal increase in processing time. Our optimized code is available online for further development and modification. The field of line connection anti-aliasing for vector maps is relatively under-explored, and our findings are pioneering in this area. The sub-optimization strategies we developed are versatile and can be applied to other situations involving complex geometric calculations, thereby providing a useful contribution to the graphics community. The ring effect anti-aliasing technique we presented can also be used to render the connection between curves, offering a novel and practical solution for this problem. The reduced processing time achieved by our solution makes it suitable for a range of applications involving vector maps, including GPS navigation, mapping services and automated driving. The optimized code we developed is versatile and can be adapted for use on a range of platforms, including desktop computers, mobile devices and embedded systems. In recent years, using multiple microphones to record conversations has become widespread, leading to an interest in demixing techniques that can separate speech from background noise on a per-channel basis. Deep learning approaches have been effective in achieving high performance in speech processing tasks, including speech separation, but applying them to multi-channel recordings requires significant computational resources and memory. To overcome this challenge, we developed a dual-path model called the DPCRN, which consists of a convolutional recurrent network (CRN) for each path and utilizes a gate to control signal flow. We found that using a smaller CRN was beneficial, as it reduced computational expenses without compromising performance. To further optimize performance, we introduced an over-lapping factor of 2 frames for the CRN, which enhanced the model's ability to capture varying frequency characteristics. Our research focuses on the conditions necessary for successful, truly entangling operations among the independent systems, and we establish a crucial threshold below which the task fails due to a previously unknown effect that arises from the interplay between the systems' correlations, their individual coupling strengths, and their initial states. Furthermore, we analyze the possibility of implementing this scenario within a chain of coupled JC systems. Our results are validated through numerical simulations. Our study also implies that in a chain, the ability to distribute genuine entanglement relies on the ability to transfer correlations between adjacent locations, a capability that breaks down at a certain threshold due to a phenomenon that could be experimentally verified. This research was motivated by previous work on a related, yet distinct scenario where the JC systems' initial states were correlated. Our findings yield a critical condition that must be met in order to succeed with that earlier proposal. In addition, our results provide a novel perspective on the earlier work, and our analysis offers a more in-depth understanding of its limitations. Our study of the earlier proposal also yields a previously unknown effect that arises from the interplay between the systems' correlations, their individual coupling strengths, and their initial states, and this effect could be experimentally verified. This paper introduces a novel task called viewport forecasting in 360-degree virtual travel videos, which predicts an user's future viewing area based on the text overlays provided with the video. High-quality 360-degree videos have several challenges related to storage and streaming, which can be alleviated by forecasting areas likely out of interest and ignoring them. To address this challenge, a dataset containing 360-degree virtual travel videos with text overlays was created, and a deep learning approach was developed to forecast viewing areas based on the overlay text and historical viewing data. Experiments on this dataset show that the forecasted viewports by the proposed method are highly similar to actual viewing areas, and the amount of data saved through viewport forecasting can be substantial. The code and dataset for this research are available at https://github.com/wh1t3p1c/vf360.

In the context of numerical simulations involving Eulerian-Lagrangian methods for particle transport, a common issue arises when dealing with large numbers of particles, particularly when using finite element or finite difference techniques. A significant challenge appears when trying to track the movement of individual particles, as many particles can end up in a single computational cell, making it difficult to accurately model their behavior and determine the effectiveness of the simulation. A new approach is proposed to address this problem by focusing on the distribution of particles within a particular scale, either in terms of spatial distance or temporal variation. By defining a set of scale-oriented approximation methods that take into account the restriction of the simulation's effectiveness, the proposed technique aims to decouple the complexity of particle transport from the spatial or temporal resolution of the simulation. As a result, the method is capable of improving the efficiency of simulations involving a large number of particles, while also enabling greater flexibility in modeling particle behavior and better representation of particle distribution. The proposed scale-oriented approximations are demonstrated to be an effective and versatile tool that can be applied to a broad range of simulations, including cases with high concentrations of particles, flowing fluids with turbulence, and particle transport across a wide range of time scales. The technique is also compared to and differentiated from other decoupling methods, such as the discrete element method and the fluid dynamics equation-based model, with the proposed approach offering greater computational efficiency and greater accuracy in modeling particle distribution. The results of the proposed method are validated through comparison with a range of reference models, including a single particle simulation, a simulation of particle transport across a wide range of time scales, and a simulation of particles flowing through a curved pipe, with the method showing excellent agreement with these models. Utilizing the Borel transform method, we analyzed both the BFKL equation and an expanded version of it, identifying relevant infrared renormalons and calculating their contributions to the distribution. A study of the resulting analytical expression was conducted to clarify the relation between tiny x values and infrared renormalons. Furthermore, we compared our results with available data on deep-inelastic scattering processes. Additionally, we explored the connection between infrared renormalons and the underlying physics of scattering processes, particularly noting that the impact of these renormalons on scattering cross-sections is influenced by the nature of the processes, i.e., whether they primarily involve hadron-hadron, hadron-nucleus, or nucleus-nucleus scattering. The effects of these renormalons on the scattering cross-sections at tiny x values are substantial, with contributions of up to 10% resulting from the interaction between the small x value and a specific infrared renormalon called the "Borel transition renormalon". Researchers are exploring the use of magnetic materials to create ultra-fast, ultra-compact photonic devices, particularly those that can operate in multiple frequency domains simultaneously. An essential component for these applications is a perfect magnetic delta-ray resonator, which has been challenging to design due to the difficulty in finding materials that meet the condition of having zero $\Delta$ for both the magnetic delta-ray and the lattice. In this study, we demonstrate the concept of a vector-sensitive magnetophotonic surface lattice, and show that a specific type of magnetic delta-ray resonator, called a $\Delta k$ resonator, can provide wide-bandwidth and simultaneous operation in multiple frequency domains. We also experimentally verify the theoretical findings in a magnetophotonic surface lattice composed of a magnetic delta-ray and a two-dimensional lattice, using micron-scale cylinders made of ferrite. The results include wide-bandwidth far-field delta-ray patterns, as well as the simultaneous generation of both a forward and backward delta-ray in the microwave frequency domain. Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through effective knowledge transfer from a more proficient agent, either via direct supervision or by observing the target agent's actions, without requiring prior knowledge about the source domain. We address the challenge of transferring knowledge in a decision-based black-box setting, where the source model's underlying architecture and performance metrics are unknown. We propose a method that enables seamless knowledge transfer through a parameter-free performance model, derived from historical action observations, which the target agent can use to guide its behavior. We demonstrate the versatility and efficacy of our approach by applying it to a wide range of tasks and domains, including complex, real-world scenarios. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in numerous evaluation metrics across multiple contexts. The code for the proposed solution as well as experimentation details are available online at: \url{https://github.com/ghulam-sabih/zero-shot-know-transfer}.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a module that has no module multiplicity, given the lattices of submodules of its composition factors, is a well-defined process. However, when the module in question has module multiplicity, its lattice is ambiguous due to undetermined joins. In such cases, we can construct lattices of submodules that have module multiplicity, but these constructions are over-determined, featuring more joins than necessary. This paper explores the relationship between these over-determined lattices and identifies their intrinsic components, specifically the lattice of submodules of the module's composition factors, modules with multiplicity, and lattice congruences with no module multiplicity. By breaking down these over-determined lattices, we can determine a set of lattice congruences that are necessary and sufficient to completely define the lattice of submodules of any module that has no module multiplicity. Although these congruences are sufficient, they are not the original defining characteristics of the module in question. Nonetheless, these congruences maintain significant importance, as they enable us to compare the lattices of submodules of different modules that have no module multiplicity. This is analogous to comparing their composition series, yet it considers the natural order of their submodules. This comparison is expressed through the lens of join-irreducible elements, which play a crucial role in determining the congruences of their lattice. This research was motivated by the study of lattice varieties, specifically the lattice of submodules of a module with no module multiplicity, as well as the variety it generates. This module variety exhibits unique properties, as it forms a lattice that is both distributive and join-semisimple. This finding is a part of the broader context of the research conducted by the authors, which aims to explore and classify the lattice varieties of module lattices with no module multiplicity. This effort involves analyzing a specific module lattice variety, as well as determining the variety of the lattice of submodules of any module that has no module multiplicity. This research provides an answer to a question initially posed by J. Almeida and B. McAlister. To facilitate seamless collaboration, agents can draw from a range of methods, including using shared rewards, proxy tasks, and co-learning without a central controller. However, most current approaches require a specialist who has expertly followed instructions and demonstrated optimal behavior. In real-world scenarios, obtaining such a specialist might be impractical or even impossible. To address this challenge, this research introduces a novel framework called Co-Observation Learning, enabling agents to collaborate without the need for a specialist who has followed explicit instructions. The framework leverages observation networks to a) enable agents to share observations and reinforce honest observation-taking, and in the process, to b) collaborate effectively. The proposed approach is tested through simulation scenarios, and the results demonstrate that cooperation is possible even without a specialist who has followed instructions, and that the framework is highly adaptable to various co-learning scenarios. This paper introduces two key metrics for evaluating error-correcting code performance: effective density and coverage. These metrics assess a code's ability to correct errors caused by sinusoidal interference. We apply and expand upon these metrics to investigate the performance of random pulse-addition code (PAC) collections and compare them to optimal code performance. Additionally, we provide a formula for calculating the coverage of a PAC code for a given interference level and discuss the code density required to correct interference of various scales. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between density and coverage for random PAC codes and determine the code density that yields the maximum coverage for a given density threshold. The exploration of underdense random PAC codes under sinusoidal interference enables us to derive an approximate formula for their coverage, which is analogous to the coverage of random pulse-addition codes in Gaussian noise. The effective density and coverage metrics prove useful in identifying the optimal code density that balances error correction and spectral efficiency in noiseless channels. The optimal density that maximizes coverage while ensuring a minimum density of one code word per $1.62/\lambda^2$ is found to be approximately $0.51/\lambda^2$ for underdense random PAC codes. The investigation of large dense random PAC codes under sinusoidal interference reveals that their coverage can be calculated using an integral, which involves the code density as a parameter. The comparison of random PAC codes and optimal PAC codes shows that the code with the maximum coverage is highly sensitive to the scaling of the interference, which makes it inferior to random PAC codes for correcting large-scale interference. Evaluating the best action space size for reinforcement learning in neural machine translation remains an open issue. We analyzed various approaches that define actions at different granularities and examined the impact of action space size on performance. Our investigation utilized a range of action definitions, incorporating strategies that leverage word frequencies, select distinct phrases, and even simple greedy methods. Our results showed that action definitions based on frequency information yield improved performance compared to traditional methods, with notable gains when combining them with techniques like teacher forcing. Interestingly, larger action spaces did not necessarily lead to better performance, and some even resulted in decline. Our study also highlighted variations in performance across different data sets and recommended a simple, high-frequency-based approach that can be useful for other machine learning tasks involving extensive action spaces. We open-sourced our code at https://github.com/ruishanwu/RLNMT.

We have examined a open system dynamics where a single photon is connected to multiple modes of a cavity that is driven periodically and not in equilibrium. The aim of this research was to investigate an important dynamical aspect of open system quantum mechanics - the time it takes for the steady state to reach a stable state. To achieve this, we developed a new method to calculate the time it takes for the steady state to reach an equilibrium state. This was done using a semi-tight-bounding technique that overestimates the change in the average state of the system over time. Furthermore, we analyzed various scenarios including strong coupling, strong driving, and both strong coupling and driving. The results of these analyses were compared to theoretical predictions made using a rotating frame of reference, as well as quantum master equations, and they showed that our overestimating method provides remarkably accurate results even in complex situations. The conclusion that can be drawn from this research is that the system's dynamics is influenced by a range of parameters including the strength of the connection between the qubit and the cavity, how strongly the cavity is driven, the time the system takes to switch between states, and the number of times the system's state changes per unit time. The results of this research have implications for using open systems in quantum information processing, and highlights the importance of carefully selecting these parameters to ensure the system remains stable. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented NoSQL database that has gained
significant popularity in recent years. As a result of its ease of use,
flexibility, and scalability, it has become a preferred choice for many
applications. Despite its success, MongoDB's transactional functionality
lacks a clear understanding, particularly in regards to its validation features
for ensuring data consistency. In essence, checking the consistency of data in
MongoDB transactions involves a complex interplay of document structures, and
requires a deep dive into the database's document-orientated nature, query
syntax, and its handling of missing values. In our work, we delve into the
inner workings of MongoDB's document structure, its query language, and its
approach to handling missing values, and then systematically break down the
process of validating the integrity of data in MongoDB transactions. We also
provide a concise and efficient algorithm for validating the consistency of
MongoDB transactions, and demonstrate its efficacy with a real-world example. 
In addition, we identify scenarios in which MongoDB's transactional feature 
falls short, and offer suggestions for improving its validation capabilities. 
Our research was conducted as part of the NIST initiative to standardize 
testing frameworks for NoSQL databases, and our findings have significant 
implications for the development of testing tools and benchmarking protocols 
for MongoDB. Our approach to validating MongoDB transactions also provides a 
valuable lesson for the development of document-oriented databases. Our work 
on MongoDB's transactional validation has been made available as an open-source 
project on GitHub, under the terms of the Apache License 2.0. Our research

has been accepted for publication in the Journal of Big Data. Our research has

A novel phenomenon associated with an adhesive strip peeling off from a surface has been uncovered. Contrary to expectations, the crackling sound emitted during removal includes patterns of quiet intervals, consistently adhering to a specific structure. These patterns can take various forms, such as sequential pairs of loud sounds, alternating loud and quiet sounds, or more complex arrangements of sounds and silences. The quiet intervals between the sounds always add up to a constant, distinctive time period. This constant time period is equivalent to half the duration of a peak sound intensity period and is independent of factors like removal speed, surface characteristics, and air conditions. The underlying mechanism responsible for this regular pattern remains unknown, posing an interesting challenge to theoretical experts in the field. Until now, researchers have focused on the rapid peeling phase as the primary cause of sound, without giving sufficient attention to the slower phase and the intricate patterns it creates. Consequently, a new approach is proposed, involving a more comprehensive analysis of the entire stripping process, including both fast and slow phase cracking sounds, their respective patterns, and the connections between them. This approach has the potential to reveal the intricate mechanisms governing the peeling process and sound generation, as well as shedding light on the complex arrangement of quiet intervals between the sounds. The novelty of this discovery also offers a distinct contribution to the study of turbulent noise, turbulence patterns, and the statistical analysis of time periods between turbulent bursts. The underlying principles can be applied to a wide range of situations involving peeling or shedding, including those on flexible or rigid surfaces, and even within living organisms, providing a better understanding of the associated sounds and the mechanisms that generate them. The proposed method can be further expanded to investigate other situations, such as the cracking sounds emitted during the removal of old stones from walls, stone shedding in mountains, or the shedding of skin cells from leaves, among others. The mathematical representation of the peeling process is based on a model that involves a series of periodic arrrangements of cracks, capable of being expanded to more complex patterns, and may be compared to other mathematical models such as the Rayleigh-Taylor instability or the Bénard-Villeret instability, among others. The proposed research offers an engaging and accessible topic for undergraduate students, providing a hands-on opportunity to conduct experiments and analyze the results, as well as offering a unique perspective on the beauty and complexity of cracking sounds. The discovery of concealed patterns in cracking sounds during shedding also raises interesting philosophical implications, inviting a reexamination of the concepts of beauty and complexity in the natural world

This paper describes the method used to analyze the beam size of the x-ray beam at the ID-29 beamline at ESRF. To precisely determine the vertical size of the x-ray beam, we utilized a scan of the x-ray beam's intensity as it moved horizontally across a highly sensitive detector. This scan, known as a "brightness scan," allows for the calculation of the x-ray beam's intensity distribution by comparing the measured scan data to simulated data based on the beam's characteristics. We developed a specialized routine to automate this process and accurately determine key beam properties, including position, orientation, divergence, and flux distribution. By validating our method using a mock scan, we demonstrated its effectiveness and identified potential limitations of the brightness scan technique. Furthermore, we analyzed various factors that influence the scan data and beam property calculations, including the effects of motion errors, detector response, and scattering of x-rays within the detector. As a result of this investigation, we were able to optimize the brightness scan procedure and reduce its duration while maintaining the accuracy of the beam property calculations. We concluded that brightness scans are a highly effective and precise method for monitoring the x-ray beam at ID-29 and other synchrotron radiation facilities equipped with variable gap undulators. These scans can be carried out in a controlled manner to minimize their impact on beam time and still provide a wealth of information about the x-ray beam, including its flux distribution, despite the complexity of the resulting data. This paper explores the optimization challenges in three distinct contexts: distributed optimization with malicious nodes, Markov decision processes, and multi-agent reinforcement learning, all involving large-scale data and extensive communication constraints. To address these issues, we develop a novel framework called Distributed Gradient Improvement (DGI), a distributed gradient-based optimization technique that converges to the solution of a given optimization problem. In DGI, nodes update their estimates using the mean gradient of the function to be optimized, with the twist that the update rule is applied to the quantized average gradient. We prove that this approach yields quantized versions of the average gradient, which converge to the solution of the underlying problem at the same rate as the ideal average gradient. We further show that DGI nodes operating under malicious assault attacks can detect the presence of malicious nodes and switch to a more robust version of the algorithm, which leads to improved convergence rates. In addition to DGI, we introduce a variant called Asymmetric DGI (A-DGI), where nodes that experience delays relative to a reference node increase their estimate based on the quantized gradient from that node. We prove that A-DGI converges under certain conditions and experimentally verify its performance in multi-agent reinforcement learning settings. We also explore the connection between DGI and A-DGI, which enables us to recover gradient descent and decentralized gradient descent as special cases of A-DGI. Finally, we conclude by outlining possible future directions and challenging problems in reinforcement learning, distributed optimization, and machine learning. Pyramid scams, also known as Ponzi schemes, have historically relied on word-of-mouth marketing to attract new investors. However, the emergence of blockchain technology allows these operations to reach a global audience with minimal costs. We analyzed the Ethereum-based Forsage project, which promoted itself as a decentralized network enabling direct investment partnerships with no fees or restrictions. Through a review of the project's code, contract interactions, and user testimonials, we uncovered evidence that Forsage is indeed a sophisticated pyramid scam utilizing standard referral marketing tactics to drive growth. We also identified risks for the majority of investors, except those at the top tier of the social network underlying the project. In fact, Forsage resembles previous iterations of pyramid scams more than novel applications of Web3 technology. With approximately $285 million in assets locked into the project at its peak, Forsage ranks among the most successful cryptocurrency scams to date. Nevertheless, as with all pyramid scams, the project is unsustainable and will eventually result in significant financial losses for the vast majority of its investors. Furthermore, we highlight the legal and tax implications faced by Forsage participants, many of whom are likely unaware of their precarious positions. Lastly, we discuss the project's demise and the likely consequences for its perpetrators and investors. The demise of Forsage serves as a prime example of how quickly Web3 scams can fall apart, with the project's decline spanning just a few months. The total losses incurred by the project and its investors are substantial, with approximately $120 million in assets frozen and an estimated total loss of $200 million including off-chain transactions. The case study of Forsage highlights the need for greater scrutiny of decentralized applications and the importance of understanding the underlying economics of blockchain-based scams. The project's success also illustrates the difficulties encountered by law enforcement in tracking down the individuals behind these operations. The financial consequences faced by Forsage participants will continue to worsen in the foreseeable future, with the project's liquidation expected to result in significant financial losses for its investors. The outcome of Forsage serves as a warning to those considering similar scams, as well as a guide for researchers studying the economics and implementation of pyramid scams within Web3. The project's code, contract interactions, and economic analysis provide a comprehensive understanding of the project's structure and operations, which can be applied to other, as-yet-unknown Web3 scams. In recent years, adversarial text generation techniques using neural networks have seen significant performance gains. A Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) consists of a generator that produces fake data and a discriminator that distinguishes between genuine and fabricated data. When used in an online setting, a trained generator can create new data that is statistically similar to existing training data, without the need for massive storage. However, generating high-quality text online proves challenging, particularly when the training data is limited. Current online text generation models often result in produced text that is far from plausible, and more often than not, requires extensive reprocessing to be coherent. We propose SparseGAN, a novel online text generation model based on a sparse adversary, that outperforms existing models in multiple evaluation metrics. SparseGAN's distinctive feature is a regularized adversary that penalizes preference for frequent training samples, leading to the generation of novel, rare samples that are more indicative of the underlying data distribution. By incorporating a mechanism to preserve generated text samples, SparseGAN demonstrates superior performance in multiple evaluation benchmarks, and the availability of pre-trained models at a smaller scale facilitates efficient deployment on resource-constrained devices. SparseGAN's capability to create rare samples at a lower frequency than current models, also enables direct evaluation through permutation importance, which confirms SparseGAN's superior performance over existing models. Alternatively, we found that the axisymmetric case can exhibit the effects of the condensate's impact on the gravitational waves through a variation in the conformal factor. Ultimately, our research indicated that the axisymmetric case and the polarized dynamics are intertwined, with the axisymmetric case representing the polarized dynamics in the context of loop quantum gravity, with the condensate's impact on the spacetime geometry and the consequent effects on the gravitational waves. As such, our findings provide a novel perspective on the relationship between the axisymmetric and polarized cases, with the axisymmetric case serving as an all-encompassing proxy for the polarized dynamics. As such, the challenge of analyzing the polarized dynamics reduces to analyzing the axisymmetric case, which, as demonstrated by our research, can be achieved through the Complex Time-Kinematic Regularization transformation, without the need for directly incorporating the quodrisaccharide condensate into the simulations. In this paper, we establish a tensor representation for a Euclidean space of any dimensionality, utilizing a specific set of geometric parameters. This representation holds true under the assumption that the dimensionality of the space is finite and natural. We derive an explicit formula to recover any vector within this Euclidean space, given its tensor representation. Furthermore, our analysis encompasses the computation of the inner product between two vectors, as well as the determination of the magnitude of a vector. We demonstrate the applicability of our tensor representation to a broad range of scenarios, including spaces with both finite and infinite dimensions, although the parameter set may need additional specifications. We also explore the relationship between our approach and other methods of vector representation, such as the polynomial representation introduced by M. K. Chorney in "Tensor Algebra for Finite Dimensional Vector Spaces", published in 2009. Additionally, we provide code implementation details for our approach. We conclude by outlining potential future work, including the application of our method to spaces with infinite dimensions and the investigation of our method's connection to the Ricci-Tsvetkov algebra. We have made our code available online at https://github.com/AhmadPourkazem/Vector-Algebra-with-Tensor-Representation. We have also presented our results at the Department of Mathematical Sciences at Purdue University in 2021. This conveys that these geometric groups possess a natural implementation of the word metric that is equivalent to a specific graph metric derived from the lattice structure, enabling us to conclude that their group algebras contain a specific subset of non-negative functions that are invariant under the lattice's action. Recent advancements in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals who are paralyzed. A two-class BCI model was developed to achieve this, and it resulted in high levels of accuracy in predicting step frequencies for both subjects.
